item.title: Mercado Bitcoin Halts Withdrawals After $40M+ Drained Across 10 Chains
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Brazil's largest crypto exchange froze deposits and withdrawals Monday after security firms tracked more than $40 million leaving its wallets.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Mercado Bitcoin says it contained a security incident early Monday, Nov 2, and paused deposits and withdrawals.
  • Hypernative estimates more than $40 million moved out across at least 10 blockchains; an Arkham analyst puts it above $46 million.
  • The exchange says no customer lost money and no data leaked. Nobody has claimed or been blamed for the theft yet.
  • Tether froze more than 4.5 million USDT tied to the incident.

More than $40 million in crypto drained out of Mercado Bitcoin's wallets early Monday, Nov 2, and Brazil's largest exchange has shut deposits and withdrawals while it works out what happened.

In a post on X, the exchange said it "identified and swiftly contained a security incident in one of our systems early this morning." It says no customer lost money and no data leaked, and Bitcoin.com News reports the transfers appear to have come from the exchange's own assets.

It hasn't said how the attacker got in. As of Monday afternoon, deposits and withdrawals were still suspended, and the exchange had given no date to reopen.

What the chain shows

Blockchain security firm Hypernative put the suspicious outflows at more than $40 million in a preliminary analysis, a figure the exchange hasn't confirmed. Arkham analyst Emmett Gallic said around 11 a.m. ET Monday that he had tracked more than $46 million and that the attacker was still sweeping old deposit addresses.

The money moved across at least 10 chains, including:

  • Bitcoin and Ethereum
  • Solana and Tron
  • Polygon, Arbitrum and Avalanche
  • BNB Smart Chain and Stellar

CoinDesk reports these were plain transfers, not a smart contract exploit. That points to someone getting hold of the exchange's signing keys or the systems that use them, which is the more worrying failure for a custodian.

Freezes and the Binance shadow

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that Tether froze more than 4.5 million USDT tied to the incident. Mercado Bitcoin also published the destination wallets so other exchanges and trackers can flag the funds.

The timing will raise eyebrows: it lands days after the more than $6 billion Binance theft the FBI pinned on North Korea's TraderTraitor. Nobody has linked the two, and no group has been named for this one.

What to do now: If you hold funds on Mercado Bitcoin, sit tight until the exchange reopens and watch its official X account for updates. Don't trust "recovery" DMs or links promising early withdrawals; phishers move fast after a hack like this. Exchanges and wallet providers should screen the published destination addresses.

item.title: Ivanti's October VPN Patch Fixed One of Three Bugs; Federal Deadline Is Today
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Ivanti has shipped fixes for the root-escalation and file-upload halves of the UTA0576 Connect Secure chain, and CISA's federal deadline for the worse one is today, Monday, November 2.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Ivanti's October 13 builds (25.1.1.2, 22.8R2.5) fixed only the auth bypass, CVE-2026-104935; the root escalation and file-upload bugs stayed open.
  • CVE-2026-111357 (privilege escalation to root) and CVE-2026-118527 (file upload) are fixed in 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 and are now on CISA's KEV list.
  • Federal agencies must remediate CVE-2026-111357 by today, November 2; Volexity says a clean Integrity Checker result doesn't prove an appliance is clean.

If you patched Ivanti Connect Secure in mid-October and moved on, your VPN was still two-thirds exposed. Ivanti revised its advisory on Thursday, October 29, to ship fixes for the other two bugs in the zero-day chain Volexity caught in early October, and CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday, October 30.

The October 13 releases, 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5, closed only CVE-2026-104935, the authentication bypass that let attackers in without credentials. The escalation to root and the file-upload step that completed the chain were still live on those builds.

The two bugs that stayed open

  • CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS 8.8 per Ivanti, 7.0 in the CVE record): the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, letting an authenticated local attacker escalate to root
  • CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS 4.3): predictable filenames let an authenticated remote attacker drop attacker-controlled content at a known path on disk

Neither looks scary alone. Chained behind an auth bypass, they're how UTA0576 went from an unauthenticated web request to root on fully patched appliances. Volexity says UTA0576 started exploiting the chain on October 3 against a 22.8R2.4 appliance, then watched the attackers pull Active Directory credentials, LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Fixed builds

Per Ivanti's October 29 guidance, as reported by Rapid7 and SecurityOnline:

  • 25.1.1.x (ISA6000/ISA8000): upgrade to 25.1.1.3
  • 22.8.x: upgrade to 25.1.1.3 or later, or 22.8R2.6 if you can't move branches yet
  • 25.1.3.0 and later (ISA4500/6500/8500): not affected
  • 22.7.x and older: not affected by this chain

The 25.1.2.x branch is affected by the original auth bypass through 25.1.2.2, with that fix in 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1, but the published version tables don't list 25.1.2.x for the two new CVEs at all. If you run it, ask Ivanti support for the remediation path in writing.

CISA's deadline for federal agencies to fix CVE-2026-111357 is today, Monday, November 2, three days after it entered the catalog. CVE-2026-118527 is due November 13. The KEV entries also point agencies to BOD 26-04 and CISA's forensic triage requirements. That's a federal clock, but anyone running these appliances should treat it as theirs.

Why a clean scan doesn't mean much

The exploit patched library code in memory and restored what it changed, and Volexity says the actor deleted entries from the ICS debug log and the Linux audit log. Volexity says Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, which looks for file changes on disk, doesn't detect this activity. Run the ICT anyway, but don't read a clean result as a clean bill of health.

What to do now:

  1. Upgrade to 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6 today, not at the next maintenance window
  2. Search proxy or WAF logs for requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi carrying an X-DSCGI-PATH header, and for bursts of rapid requests to that path
  3. Pull Volexity's IOCs from its GitHub threat-intel repo and check them against logs stored off the appliance
  4. If anything hits, assume domain credentials are burned: rotate the appliance's LDAP service account, LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, and hunt for lateral movement from the VPN's IP

Ivanti's VPN has now needed two emergency patch rounds for one campaign in just over two weeks. If you're still on 22.8, Ivanti's own guidance is to move to 25.1.1.3 or later, with 22.8R2.6 as the stopgap. This is a decent week to schedule that migration.

item.title: Lumen Maps Volt Typhoon's 'Silent Train' Relay Built on Four Zero-Days
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Black Lotus Labs says the China-linked group chains hijacked routers and enterprise boxes into relay paths up to six hops deep, and rebuilds a burned chain in under two minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Lumen's Black Lotus Labs documented Silent Train, the relay framework it ties to Volt Typhoon, built from 27+ classes of hijacked devices.
  • Four confirmed zero-day campaigns feed it (N-able N-central, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, VeloCloud Orchestrator, Versa Director) plus a likely one in Quest KACE.
  • Targets include telecoms, defense contractors, MSPs and water, energy and transport operators.
  • Patch management platforms first, pull admin interfaces off the internet, and hunt for living-off-the-land activity on them.

Volt Typhoon doesn't need a botnet that survives takedowns. It needs a fresh path to your network, and according to Lumen it can assemble one from someone else's routers in under two minutes.

Lumen's Black Lotus Labs published research on Wednesday, October 28 describing what it calls Silent Train: not a single malware family, but an operational framework the China-linked group uses to route sessions through compromised devices before touching a victim.

How the relay works

Sessions start on a VPS outside the US, bounce through an average of four non-US nodes, then enter US IP space and make more hops before reaching the target. Up to six hops can sit between the operator and the victim.

The nodes come from more than 27 device classes. Lumen names consumer and small-office gear like TP-Link routers and Netgear Orbi mesh systems alongside enterprise platforms from Fortinet, Cisco and CyberPanel.

Each session touches one to five victims, often just one organization. Lumen says it has sent hundreds of victim notifications over three years.

The zero-days feeding it

Lumen links four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one to the framework:

  • N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876)
  • Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS 10.0)
  • VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812)
  • Versa Director (CVE-2024-39717), exploited in mid-2024
  • Quest KACE, a zero-day Lumen assesses with moderate confidence, with no CVE named and more than 30 victims

Look at that list. Almost every entry is a management or control-plane product: the box that pushes config to everything else. Own one and you inherit the trust relationships of every network it manages, including an MSP's downstream customers.

Lumen is careful about what it can't see. Its telemetry couldn't always distinguish a known bug from an undisclosed one, and it calls the geographic clustering of activity unclear. Volt Typhoon itself is a formally attributed PRC state actor, named by CISA, the NSA and the FBI in advisory AA24-038A.

What to do now

  1. Patch centralized management platforms before anything else, starting with the products above.
  2. Take admin interfaces off the internet and put them behind a VPN, jump host or management network.
  3. Centralize logs from those systems and keep them longer than you think you need.
  4. Hunt for unusual admin logins, remote file transfers and built-in tools run in bursts on management hosts.
  5. Replace end-of-life routers on your perimeter that no longer get firmware.

Worth checking today: if an MSP manages your network, ask which of these platforms it runs and when it patched them.

item.title: Binance Reopens Withdrawals in Phases, Says 95% of Stolen Crypto Covered
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Binance restarted withdrawals network by network on Sunday, starting with bitcoin, and as of Monday has 15 networks open, another phase due Tuesday and about 95% of the stolen crypto replaced.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Phase one opened Sunday, Nov. 1, at 06:00 UTC with bitcoin and reached 15 networks by midday UTC.
  • As of Monday, withdrawals aren't fully back; Binance is still testing the rest, with the next phase scheduled for Tuesday.
  • Binance says it has covered about 95% of the roughly $6.3 billion stolen with its own funds, up from 90% on Saturday.
  • Expect phishing dressed up as withdrawal or compensation notices; trust only Binance's own site and verified accounts.

Binance customers can move money out again, on most major networks. The exchange restarted withdrawals on Sunday, Nov. 1, in a window that opened at 06:00 UTC, with bitcoin first, per CoinDesk.

More followed within hours. By 12:36 UTC Sunday, all 15 networks in the first phase were live, according to UPI. Bitcoin Magazine lists them as bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, XRP, Dogecoin, Tron, Polygon, Avalanche, Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Zcash, TON and Sui.

How the restart works

This is a phased reopening, not a switch flipped back on. Binance says each blockchain has to pass its own security and stability checks before withdrawals resume, and it is prioritizing the networks customers ask for most.

As of Monday, withdrawals are not fully back. Binance says it is still testing the remaining networks and assets, and Bitcoin Magazine reports the next phase is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3, with details to follow.

Deposits have stayed open through the restart, per The National and Bitcoin Magazine.

Customers did pull money. Between 06:00 and 15:30 UTC Sunday, Binance processed about $4.65 billion in withdrawals against $1.01 billion in deposits, a net outflow of roughly $3.64 billion. That's about 2.1% of the $171 billion in assets in its late-October proof of reserves, per Bitcoin Magazine.

The money

Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the stolen assets with company money, including its Secure Asset Fund for Users. That's up from 90% on Saturday. The last 5% is less liquid tokens outside its top ten listed assets that take longer to buy in size, per CoinDesk.

The exchange still puts the theft at about $6.3 billion. About $3 billion has been frozen, mostly stablecoins their issuers could block, per CoinDesk. On Saturday the FBI formally attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor unit and said the thieves were converting assets to ether for laundering through DeFi and instant swap services.

Getting withdrawals back within about three days of the largest crypto theft on record is a real operational win. The harder part is still open. Binance has said a compromised engineer's laptop was involved and that it later found additional points of breach, but as of Monday it hasn't published a full post-mortem, per Bitcoin Magazine.

What to do now: if you have funds on Binance, check the app or Binance's official announcements for which networks are open before you try to withdraw, and don't pay anyone who offers to speed things up. Expect scammers to push fake "withdrawal restart" and "compensation" links, so ignore DMs and only trust binance.com and Binance's verified accounts.

item.title: FBI Officially Blames North Korea's TraderTraitor for $6B Binance Theft
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Two days after the record Binance heist, the FBI says North Korea did it and is asking exchanges, DeFi services and node operators to block the stolen funds.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • The FBI says North Korea's TraderTraitor actors stole more than $6 billion from Binance on or about October 29.
  • It's the first government attribution; until now, the North Korea link came from TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
  • The FBI says the funds are mostly being converted to Ethereum and expects them to move through DeFi and instant-swap services next.
  • Crypto businesses should block the addresses the FBI published; Binance users should watch for fake withdrawal and refund notices.

It's official now. The FBI said in a cyber alert Saturday that North Korea "was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets" from Binance, according to Newsweek, pinning the largest crypto heist on record on the regime's TraderTraitor actors.

That moves the attribution from analytics firms to the US government. On Friday, TRM Labs and Chainalysis had already tied the theft to TraderTraitor, but Binance hadn't named anyone and the FBI had only said it was engaged with partners.

The FBI moved fast. The theft happened on or about Thursday, October 29, and the alert landed two days later. TraderTraitor is the same cluster the Bureau blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

Where the money is going

According to the FBI, the hackers are mainly converting the stolen assets into Ethereum. The Bureau expects the next leg to run through decentralized finance platforms and instant-swap services, per the Associated Press.

Expect a long tail. Crypto expert Ari Redbord told the AP he expects the funds to be split up and laundered through smaller exchanges over months.

The FBI is asking crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, DeFi services and node operators to block transactions tied to a list of attacker addresses it published with the alert.

Binance's side

Binance has said a software engineer's compromised laptop was part of how the attacker got in, and that it later found more points of breach. It has promised to repay customers in full, per the AP.

Withdrawals are moving again. Binance began reopening them in phases on Sunday, Nov. 1, at 06:00 UTC, and by Monday 15 networks were back, with another phase scheduled for Tuesday, per Bitcoin Magazine. The exchange now says it has covered about 95% of the stolen assets, up from 90% on Saturday.

What to do now: if you run an exchange, bridge, swap service or RPC node, load the FBI's address list into your screening and block matches. If you're a Binance user, expect phishing dressed up as "withdrawal restart" or "compensation" notices, and trust only Binance's own site and verified accounts.

item.title: Northflank Breach Exposes Customer Secrets as AI Keys Get Abused
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cloud host Northflank told every customer to assume their environment variables were decrypted, and users have already caught stolen AI API keys being spent, making it at least the ninth AI developer platform hit in October.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Northflank says customers should assume all environment variables were decrypted and rotate every key.
  • Multiple users confirmed their AI API keys stored on the platform were used without permission.
  • Wiz counts at least nine AI developer platforms with incidents in October, with no single shared bug found yet.
  • If you host on Northflank, revoke AI provider keys at the provider, rotate database secrets, and check billing logs.

If you run anything on Northflank, treat every secret in it as burned. The cloud hosting platform told customers on Friday, October 30, to assume their environment variables were decrypted and to "disable/rotate all keys," after Wiz flagged suspicious activity at 11:43 UTC.

By that evening, multiple users had confirmed their AI API keys stored on Northflank were being used by someone else. In a Monday, November 2 update, Northflank said it believes the attack was contained within an hour of the first alert, that running workloads and their data show no sign of access, and that the attacker appears to have targeted secrets in its control plane. It still hasn't said how the attacker got in or how many customers are affected.

What Northflank has done

The company's status page shows engineers pushing network policy patches within about 20 minutes of the Wiz alert, then bringing in Wiz's incident response team. Since then it has added tooling so customers can actually clean up:

  • Secret rotation for PostgreSQL and MongoDB addons (Friday afternoon UTC)
  • Audit logs for every customer, free tier included (early Saturday UTC)
  • Secret rotation for MySQL and Redis (Saturday, October 31)
  • Secret rotation for MinIO and RabbitMQ addons (late Saturday UTC)

Monday's update moved the incident to monitoring. Independent forensic auditors are reviewing it, and Northflank promises a root cause analysis once findings are confirmed. It says it patched CVE-2026-98432 across its fleet, though it doesn't say that bug was the way in.

It also revoked access tokens, sessions, VCS integrations and cross-account IAM roles where it could, so customers need to sign in again and reconnect integrations. Its advice hasn't changed: rotate everything, starting with AI provider keys. A company that tells you to assume decryption is telling you it can't rule it out.

Part of a bad month for AI dev platforms

Northflank is the latest entry in what Wiz calls "Black October." Its researchers count at least nine AI developer platforms that disclosed incidents in October, including Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, OpenCode, Railway, Warp, and Zeabur. Several point to credential access, and a few describe an "agent swarm" style attack.

Wiz is careful here, and you should be too. It hasn't found a single vulnerability or dependency tying the incidents together, and it doesn't claim one crew is behind all of them.

What it does show is how fast stolen AI keys get monetized: in two separate cases it tracked, attackers validated keys within 30 minutes and then ran up more than $100,000 in Amazon Bedrock usage at list price. Those two cases aren't linked to Northflank.

What to do now: Revoke and replace any AI provider keys you stored on Northflank at the provider itself, not just in the platform. Rotate database and addon secrets, switch off public access on addons you don't need exposed, and pull your provider usage and billing logs back to October 30.

Sign back in to Northflank and reconnect your Git integrations. Then turn on spend limits with your AI providers so the next leaked key has a ceiling.

item.title: Chainalysis Breached by Attacker Using AI Agents; Customer Names Exposed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The blockchain analytics firm says an outside attacker got into its systems and internal tools and took customer user IDs, names, emails and role labels, but not investigation data.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Chainalysis confirmed a cybersecurity incident on Friday, Oct. 30, and has notified all customers.
  • Reported exposure: user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels; no investigation data, passwords, MFA secrets or session tokens so far.
  • Customers should expect targeted phishing: treat unexpected password resets and login prompts as hostile and turn on 2FA.

The company that helps police trace stolen crypto just had its own systems broken into. Chainalysis said Friday that it was "the target of a cybersecurity incident" and that it has notified all of its customers.

According to the details Chainalysis gave customers, as reported by Cyber Security News, TokenPost and Blockchain.News, an outside attacker used "offensive agentic techniques" to get into its systems and internal tools. That's a fancy way of saying AI agents did at least some of the work. Chainalysis hasn't explained what that looked like.

What was taken, and what wasn't

The data reported as accessed covers customers and the people inside their organizations:

  • Platform user IDs
  • Full names
  • Email addresses
  • Organization role labels

Chainalysis calls that data non-sensitive. Its public notice says it has found no evidence of access to investigation content, authentication credentials or session tokens. Reports on the customer notice add graphs, notes, cases, transaction and query results, plaintext passwords and MFA secrets to the not-touched list.

The company says it's still working out which records belong to which customer organization and has brought in outside security experts. It also says the incident isn't related to the multibillion-dollar Binance theft it has been helping trace in recent days.

Why "non-sensitive" undersells it

Chainalysis customers include government agencies, law enforcement and crypto exchanges. A list of who works there, their emails and what role each person holds is a ready-made phishing target list, and some of the people best positioned to want it are the crypto thieves those customers chase.

As of Monday, plenty is still missing, and Chainalysis has posted no update to its notice. There's no count of affected users or organizations, no entry point, no named attacker and no timeline beyond detection sometime in October. The notice also says the incident resembles others at tech platforms in recent weeks without naming them, and Chainalysis declined to answer follow-up questions from The Block.

What to do now: if your organization uses Chainalysis, assume staff names, emails and roles are in an attacker's hands. Warn those users about targeted phishing, treat any unexpected password reset or login prompt as hostile, and make sure two-factor authentication is on for every account.

item.title: Florida Aid Site Breach May Have Exposed SSNs of 4.9 Million People
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anyone who ever applied for Florida student financial aid may have had their Social Security number, birth date and address taken, and the state is offering no credit monitoring.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Florida's Department of Education says the Student Financial Aid website was breached; staff learned of it on October 19.
  • About 4.9 million past applicants may be affected, with SSNs, birth dates, addresses, phones and emails potentially exposed.
  • Aid payments aren't affected, but the notice offers no credit monitoring.
  • Freeze your credit at all three bureaus if you or your kids ever applied for Florida aid.

If you, or your kids, ever applied for financial aid in Florida, treat your Social Security number as exposed.

The Florida Department of Education disclosed on Thursday, October 29, that attackers got into the Florida Student Financial Aid website. It puts the number of people potentially affected at about 4.9 million, and says anyone who has previously applied for financial aid in Florida may be affected.

What was taken

The department's notice lists these fields as potentially exposed:

  • Social Security numbers
  • First and last names
  • Dates of birth
  • Home addresses
  • Phone numbers, including mobile
  • Email addresses
  • Gender codes

That's a complete identity-theft kit. Not everyone's record holds every field, the department says, but the SSN plus birth date combination is the part that matters.

Staff became aware of the intrusion on October 19, about ten days before the public notice. The aid website has been taken down, The Record reports, and the department warns other online services may be disrupted while it recovers.

What the state isn't saying

The department won't describe the attack or the attackers, calling it an ongoing criminal investigation with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Florida Digital Service. It says it believes the incident was limited to the aid site and that it acted to contain it and secure its systems.

As of Monday, its notice still offers no credit monitoring. The notice points people to free credit reports, the three bureaus and the FTC, and routes questions to an email inbox rather than a call center. For a breach this size, involving a lot of young people with thin credit files, that's a thin response.

Current aid, disbursements, tuition payments and scholarship eligibility are not affected, according to the department.

What to do now

  1. Freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It's free and takes minutes online.
  2. Freeze credit for any minor children who applied, too; their files are prime targets because nobody checks them.
  3. Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and look for accounts you didn't open.
  4. Treat calls, texts or emails about Florida financial aid with suspicion, since attackers now have the details to make them convincing.

item.title: NetamLoader Hid in Windows' Update Folder Inside a Patch My PC Package
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Kaspersky found a stealthy .NET loader in the Windows update folder of an apparent government machine in Asia, riding a legitimate Patch My PC runner and a Microsoft-signed DLL to load its payload.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Kaspersky's NetamLoader was found in a CAB archive in C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download, next to real Patch My PC components.
  • It uses AppDomainManager injection through a Microsoft-signed DLL, patches AMSI, disables CLR ETW logging and wipes its own files, Prefetch and update log entries.
  • One victim, in Asia, apparently on a custom Windows 10 build used by government agencies; Kaspersky ties it to no known group.
  • Watch for stray .config files beside signed binaries in the update download folder.

The folder Windows uses to stage updates is about the last place an admin goes looking for malware. That's exactly where Kaspersky found NetamLoader.

In a Securelist write-up published Thursday, October 29, Kaspersky says its telemetry flagged a .config file using AppDomainManager injection. It sat inside a CAB archive under C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download, surrounded by mostly legitimate Patch My PC files. The first review missed it; a second pass found the infection chain.

How the chain runs

The host process is Patch My PC's own PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe, launched with -updatepackage. From there, everything is borrowed from trusted code:

  • A planted PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config and fabric.config trigger AppDomainManager injection via the Microsoft-signed Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll
  • A crafted Resources.resx is parsed with ResXResourceSet and deserialized through BinaryFormatter
  • XAML payloads load via XamlReader
  • The final stage is loaded into dllhost.exe through a remote COM object

Once running, it patches AMSI's scan function, turns off CLR ETW logging with an environment variable, and deletes the planted config and resource files, CLR usage logs, Prefetch files and matching update-agent log entries. It sleeps 20 to 40 minutes between steps and runs a watchdog of roughly 28 hours, which is long enough to outlast most sandboxes.

Command and control runs over HTTPS to openaigpt4v[.]com, with the client set to trust any certificate. Traffic is AES-128-CBC with an HMAC, and the beacon goes quiet for 22 to 28 hours if it doesn't get a valid answer.

Who and how

Kaspersky saw a single victim in Asia. A log path points to a customized Windows 10 build that Kaspersky says may be used by a government there. The Record describes the attackers as suspected nation-state hackers, but Kaspersky couldn't link the tooling to any known group.

How the package got onto the machine is the open question. Kaspersky says the setup strongly indicates a supply-chain attack aimed at that custom Windows build, but it didn't see how the CAB was delivered, and nothing in the report says Patch My PC itself was compromised. The runner is simply a trusted signed binary that will load a config file sitting next to it.

What to hunt for: unexpected .config files beside signed executables in SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install, the COMPlus_ETWEnabled variable being set, unexpected GUID-named keys with a DllSurrogate value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID, sudden Prefetch or CLR log deletions, and any traffic to the C2 domain or 104.18.14[.]219. Kaspersky's post lists file hashes for the CAB, configs and each payload layer.

item.title: Judge Won't Require a Privacy Watchdog in Character.AI's Bankruptcy Sale
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The DOJ's bankruptcy watchdog says Character.AI's privacy policy may let it sell chat histories, but the Delaware judge only encouraged the company to appoint a privacy ombudsman.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • The DOJ's U.S. Trustee Program objected on October 27 that Character.AI's privacy policy is ambiguous and may allow chat histories to be sold.
  • The policy was updated July 1, while the company was already trying to sell its assets.
  • On October 30 the judge approved the auction rules and declined to require a consumer privacy ombudsman, only strongly encouraging one.
  • If you used Character.AI, delete chats you wouldn't want a new owner to read.

About 12 million people a month use Character.AI, according to the U.S. Trustee's filing, and a lot of what they typed was personal. Now those chats sit in a bankruptcy estate, and nobody is required to referee what happens to them.

At a hearing on Friday, October 30, a Delaware bankruptcy judge declined to order Character.AI to bring in a consumer privacy ombudsman, according to MLex. The judge only "strongly encourage[d]" the company to consider one, and approved the rules for auctioning its assets.

The DOJ's objection

The push came from the Justice Department's U.S. Trustee Program, which oversees bankruptcy cases. Its October 27 filing, reported by The Record, calls the company's privacy policy "ambiguous" and says it suggests at least some users' chat histories can be sold.

The timing bothers the trustee too. Character.AI updated that policy on July 1, while it was "actively seeking to sell its assets."

The filing flags these kinds of data as especially sensitive:

  • Personally identifiable information
  • Data from minors
  • Health and demographic details users shared
  • Anything users would reasonably expect to stay private

An ombudsman would advise the court on what can be sold and on what terms. The court could restrict or block a data transfer either way, but without one there's no independent voice in the room arguing for users.

States are watching

In mid-October, attorneys general from 39 states and D.C. filed a notice in the case asking that privacy and safety protections be built into any sale. They argue the company's voluntary limits on minors are not compulsory, are incomplete and could be reversed by a future buyer. The states also objected to the auction rules, which the judge approved anyway.

We've seen this play before. 23andMe's bankruptcy turned genetic data into an asset on the auction block, and the fight over consent dominated the case. Chat logs with an AI companion are arguably more intimate than DNA, because people chose to write them.

Disney, which hired most of Character.AI's staff before the filing, is the opening bidder at $20 million. That bid buys a non-exclusive license to some of the company's technology, and Disney says it isn't buying user data or personal information. Rival bids are due November 20, so as of Monday nobody knows who could end up with the chat logs.

What to do now: if you or your kids used Character.AI, save anything you want to keep, then delete the conversations you wouldn't want a stranger to inherit. Deleting before a sale won't guarantee every copy is gone, but it's the main control users have.

item.title: GM Pays States $220 Million for Selling Smart Driver Data to Insurers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A coalition of 36 state attorneys general says GM sold drivers' braking, speeding and trip data through brokers to insurers for years while telling drivers it wouldn't share it with insurers without consent.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • GM agreed to pay $220 million to a coalition of 36 attorneys general over its Smart Driver program, run from 2016 to 2024.
  • Trip times, hard braking, rapid acceleration and speeding data went to brokers and then insurers, who could raise premiums.
  • The OnStar app wrongly told more than 370,000 drivers they weren't enrolled; their data stayed with brokers.
  • GM now needs express consent and must minimize driving data, but drivers get no restitution and the terms don't claw back data already sold.

If you were enrolled in Smart Driver, your car logged every time you braked hard. For eight years, the states say, GM sold that data to brokers who passed it to the companies that set insurance rates.

General Motors will pay $220 million to settle claims from a coalition of 36 attorneys general over its Smart Driver program, the states announced on Thursday, October 29. Details below come from the New York AG's announcement.

What GM collected and where it went

From 2016 to 2024, Smart Driver tracked:

  • Trip counts and start and end times
  • Hard braking
  • Rapid acceleration
  • Speeding

GM sold that data to data brokers under contracts saying it would be used for insurance products, the states say. The brokers sold it on to insurers, who could adjust premiums. All the while, GM told drivers it wouldn't share their data with insurers without express consent.

Most drivers were signed up at the dealership when they bought the car, and in many cases staff allegedly accepted the terms for customers without their consent. From 2020 to 2024, staff earned bonuses tied partly to sign-ups and dealers were ranked on enrollment numbers. New York alone had more than 700,000 drivers in the program.

The worst detail: GM's OnStar app told more than 370,000 drivers they weren't enrolled when they were. GM later unenrolled them quietly, and the data it had already sold stayed with the brokers and insurers.

What the settlement changes

GM must get affirmative express consent before collecting or sharing driving behavior and location data, collect less of it, run a privacy program with internal and outside assessments, and train dealers not to enroll people without approval. New York's share is about $12 million; Michigan gets about $7.2 million and Massachusetts $5.7 million. None of it goes back to drivers as restitution, though a nationwide private class action seeking money is still pending, according to Michigan's AG.

GM killed Smart Driver in 2024 after the New York Times exposed it, so the forward-looking terms mostly lock in what it already stopped. Nothing in the announced terms pulls the data back from the insurers that bought it. Texas, which sued separately in 2024 and wants GM ordered to delete the data, isn't part of this deal.

If you were enrolled in Smart Driver, you can ask the data brokers that supply insurers for your consumer disclosure file to see what they hold on your driving.

item.title: RHEL Patches Linux TCP Flaw CVE-2026-98432, but Ubuntu LTS Still Waits
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Red Hat shipped fixed kernels for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 on November 1, but Ubuntu's LTS releases still had no fix for the 9.8-rated IPv4 TCP use-after-free as of Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • CVE-2026-98432 is a race in IPv4 TCP connection setup that can cause a use-after-free; it dates back to Linux 4.4.
  • Upstream fixed it October 5; Debian, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux and now RHEL 8, 9 and 10 have patched kernels.
  • Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 still had no fixed kernel as of Monday, November 2.
  • No attacks or KEV listing so far, but Anthropic says its model built a working remote root exploit.

Red Hat shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 on Sunday, November 1. Ubuntu's LTS releases still don't have one as of Monday, four weeks after the upstream fix landed on October 5.

The bug is a race condition in how the kernel sets up IPv4 TCP connections, which can leave it reading memory it already freed. It's been there since Linux 4.4. IPv6 isn't affected. The kernel's CVE team scored it 9.8 on October 24.

Who has a fix

As of Monday, according to vendor trackers and errata:

  • Red Hat: RHEL 8 (RHSA-2026:93414), RHEL 9 (RHSA-2026:93412) and RHEL 10 (RHSA-2026:93413) fixed November 1; RHEL 9 real-time kernels and OpenShift 4 still waiting; RHEL 7 not affected
  • Ubuntu: 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10 fix in progress; 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04 vulnerable
  • Debian: trixie fixed October 16, bookworm October 17 and 22
  • Oracle Linux: UEK kernels fixed October 16
  • Amazon Linux 2 and 2023: fixed kernels released between October 24 and 30
  • SUSE: Linux Micro 6.2, openSUSE Leap 16.0 and SLES 16.0 fixed; SLES 15 SP7 still in progress

Upstream stable kernels with the fix include 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3.

The scores moved

Red Hat now rates the bug Critical at 9.8, matching the kernel CVE team, after scoring it between 5.9 and 8.1 last week. As of October 29, Oracle and SUSE said 8.1 and Amazon 7.0, according to The Hacker News. A race you have to win over the network is harder than a one-packet bug, and vendors weighed that differently.

The reason nobody should relax is Anthropic. The company said on October 27 that its model wrote a working root exploit against servers with a multipath TCP listener, leaking a kernel address in 48 minutes and reaching code execution five minutes later.

Anthropic hasn't released the code, and CloudLinux says its kernel team couldn't reproduce the claim. As of Monday there are no reports of attacks in the wild, and the bug isn't in CISA's KEV catalog.

There's no clean workaround either. Red Hat's October 30 security bulletin offers an interim nftables rule that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options, but says it only reduces exposure, may disrupt workloads and doesn't replace the kernel update. Go's security team says GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 turns off MPTCP in Go programs but calls that fragile, and stresses the bug isn't MPTCP-specific.

What to do now:

  1. Patch and reboot now on RHEL 8, 9 and 10, Debian, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux and openSUSE Leap 16.0
  2. On Ubuntu, watch Canonical's CVE tracker and schedule a reboot window for the day the kernel lands
  3. If you build your own kernels, move to one of the fixed stable releases above
  4. Inventory internet-facing services that accept MPTCP, and use Livepatch or kpatch where your vendor ships one

item.title: Progress Fixes 15 WS_FTP Server Flaws, One Leaking Admin Credentials
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Progress disclosed 15 bugs in WS_FTP Server for Windows, including a CVSS 10 flaw that lets unauthenticated attackers pull administrative credentials, and only the newest builds fix all of them.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • CVE-2026-84295 (CVSS 10) lets an unauthenticated attacker read sensitive data, including admin credentials.
  • Six of the 15 flaws are rated critical, including a 9.9 command injection; as of Monday none are known to be exploited or in CISA's KEV catalog.
  • Go to 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4: the earlier 2024.0.6 and 2025.0.3 builds fix only 3 of the 15.
  • WS_FTP was exploited within days of a fix in 2023, so don't wait for a KEV listing.

An unauthenticated attacker who can reach a vulnerable WS_FTP Server can walk away with its administrative credentials. That's CVE-2026-84295, rated a perfect 10, and it leads a list of 15 WS_FTP Server vulnerabilities Progress Software disclosed on Thursday, October 29.

The fixes themselves shipped earlier. On the 2025 line, Progress released 2025.0.3 on September 3 and 2025.0.4 on October 1, according to its release notes.

The bugs affect WS_FTP Server on Windows. Six are critical, three high and six medium, according to SecurityOnline's breakdown of the advisory. As of Monday, there's no confirmed exploitation, no public exploit code and none of the 15 is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The critical ones

These are the bugs worth losing sleep over:

  • CVE-2026-84295 (10.0): improper authentication exposing admin credentials, no login needed
  • CVE-2026-90868 (9.9): OS command injection on the Windows host, needs a low-privilege account and only works under certain configurations
  • CVE-2026-90863 (9.1): missing authorization in the administrative interface
  • CVE-2026-90864 and CVE-2026-90866 (9.1): path traversal
  • CVE-2026-90865 (9.0): another OS command injection

The rest include two multi-factor authentication bypasses (CVE-2026-84296 and CVE-2026-90862), two denial-of-service bugs and a cleartext password leak.

Chain the top two and the picture gets ugly. CVE-2026-90868 needs an account, and CVE-2026-84295 can hand admin credentials to anyone who reaches an unpatched server.

Two builds, two batches

This is where admins can trip up. The fixes landed in two groups:

  • 2024.0.6 and 2025.0.3 fix CVE-2026-84294, CVE-2026-84295 and CVE-2026-84296
  • 2024.0.7 and 2025.0.4 fix the other 12

If you moved to 2025.0.3 or 2024.0.6 and stopped there, you're still exposed to the command injection bugs. If you're already on 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4, you have every fix.

Why speed matters here

WS_FTP has been here before. In 2023, attackers began exploiting a deserialization flaw in its Ad Hoc Transfer module (CVE-2023-40044) three days after Progress patched it, months after Progress's MOVEit Transfer was hit in a mass data-theft campaign. File transfer servers hold exactly the data extortion crews want, and Censys counted about 2,500 WS_FTP Server hosts reachable from the internet on October 29.

What to do now:

  1. Upgrade to 2024.0.7 or 2025.0.4, not the earlier builds
  2. Pull the web admin console off the internet and restrict it to internal networks
  3. Rotate WS_FTP admin passwords after patching, since CVE-2026-84295 exposes them
  4. Review admin logins and recently created accounts for anything you don't recognize

item.title: CrowdStrike: China's Vapor Panda Ran AI Agents Against 200+ Organizations
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CrowdStrike says a China state-backed group used the ARTEX agent framework on DeepSeek to target foreign ministries, defense firms and telecoms across 14 countries in under two weeks, mostly through old, boring weaknesses.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • CrowdStrike links a campaign against 200+ organizations since October 17 to Vapor Panda, using the ARTEX agentic pentest framework running mainly on DeepSeek.
  • The agents didn't need zero-days: unsigned SAML, an XXE bug, an unauthenticated orchestration service, never-rotated keys and password spraying did the work.
  • Hunt for artx/artex in command lines and cloud role names, the C:\ProgramData\artx5v\ folder, and the C2 domains in CrowdStrike's report.

Forty commands an hour is what CrowdStrike used to see from a human operator on a keyboard. With the agent framework behind a new China-linked campaign, CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers told CyberScoop, that could top 1,500.

That framework is ARTEX, which CrowdStrike says the state-backed group it tracks as Vapor Panda ran against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries starting October 17. Targets included foreign ministries, a European presidency and prime minister's office, defense and intelligence agencies, think tanks and telecom providers. CrowdStrike published the report on Thursday, October 29, and CyberScoop reported the next day that the campaign was still active.

How the agents worked

ARTEX uses a main agent that hands work to planner and worker agents, all sharing one graph of facts, findings and goals. The operation ran mostly on DeepSeek, plus a second subscription-based commercial model that CrowdStrike says it couldn't identify.

The interesting part is what the agents exploited. None of it is exotic:

  • Unsigned SAML assertions combined with an XXE flaw, used to pull a role from the cloud instance metadata service
  • An unauthenticated orchestration service that gave root in a container environment
  • Keys from a 2022 directory export, still usable enough to forge an admin token
  • VPN configs pulled from a user's sent mail, and a VPN client key from a May 2024 email leak
  • Plain password spraying against government, think tank and corporate accounts

Once inside, the playbook was familiar: LAPS passwords, resource-based constrained delegation abuse, and the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor loaded through a renamed GameHook binary. The operator also told the agents to find Windows hosts without a Falcon sensor and focus there. The agents just made that search faster.

How sure is anyone

CrowdStrike says it linked the controller to Vapor Panda infrastructure and confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations. CrowdStrike told CyberScoop a much higher figure: about 70% of targets confirmed compromised or showing signs of a successful intrusion, at moderate confidence. Those two numbers measure different things, and the confirmed one is the one to quote.

CrowdStrike says this is separate from the ARTEX campaign Microsoft pinned on a group it tracks as Storm-0940, which hit Microsoft 365 tenants of ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in mid-October. ARTEX is reported to be open source and able to work with any AI model, so two China-nexus clusters on the same framework in one month shouldn't surprise anyone. Expect more.

The lesson isn't that AI found new bugs. It's that agents make it cheap to try every old one, everywhere, at once. Debt you've been carrying for years (unrotated keys, permissive SAML, an internal service with no auth) now gets found in days.

What to do now:

  1. Search EDR and cloud logs for command lines containing artx or artex, cloud roles prefixed artx, comments containing art18-, and the C:\ProgramData\artx5v\ directory
  2. Block and hunt for the C2 domains and GameHook-related hashes in CrowdStrike's IOC table
  3. Enforce SAML signature validation and require IMDSv2 on cloud instances
  4. Rotate signing keys and service credentials that appear in old backups or directory exports
  5. Put EDR on internal-only hosts too, since that's exactly where these agents went looking

item.title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Read Your Private Chats Until October 26
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Parameter researchers chained a MathLive postMessage handler and a CSP bypass so that opening a public ChatGPT share link ran their JavaScript in the viewer's logged-in session; OpenAI has fixed it and paid $5,000.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Opening a crafted public ChatGPT share link could run attacker JavaScript as chatgpt.com, list the viewer's chats and read private ones.
  • The chain used a MathLive postMessage listener that accepted any origin and injected raw HTML, plus a CSP bypass via a YouTube oEmbed JSONP endpoint.
  • OpenAI fixed both web frontends by October 26; there's nothing for users to patch, and no in-the-wild abuse has been reported.

One click on a ChatGPT share link was enough to hand a stranger your chat history. Researchers at Parameter showed that a public /share/ page could run their JavaScript inside the viewer's own logged-in session, list recent conversations, read one that had never been shared, and ship it to an outside server.

OpenAI has fixed it. Parameter reported the bug through OpenAI's bounty program on October 18, and both of ChatGPT's web frontends were patched by October 26. The payout was $5,000, and Parameter published its write-up on Wednesday, October 28, after the fix.

How the chain worked

No single bug did this. It took three pieces lining up:

  1. The attacker publishes a share containing a graph, which loads the MathLive math-input library
  2. MathLive's postMessage listener accepted messages from any origin and wrote raw HTML into the page
  3. A later HTML Preview block in the same share sends those messages, and a YouTube oEmbed JSONP endpoint on the allowlist gets the script past ChatGPT's content security policy

In one version the victim had to click Preview once. In another, the block was flagged as previewable and ran on page load. From there the script could call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, which Parameter fairly describes as account takeover.

Why this one stings

Share links are built to be clicked by people who don't know the sender. They show up in Slack threads, Reddit posts and support tickets. A bug that turns one into a session hijack hits exactly the behavior the feature encourages.

It's also a reminder that chat apps now render a lot more than text. Math, graphs, live HTML previews: every renderer is attack surface, and third-party libraries like MathLive bring their own message handlers along. The postMessage bug here is a decade-old web mistake, not an AI problem.

OpenAI's triage moved fast once it engaged. It reproduced the issue and raised it from P2 to P1 within three days, then shipped CSP changes before the full fix. Five thousand dollars for a one-click read of any user's private chats feels light, though.

What to do now: nothing on the user side, since the fix was server-side. If your company lets staff paste sensitive work into ChatGPT, this is a good prompt to check whether you're on an enterprise workspace with retention controls, and to treat share links from outside your org like any other unknown link.

item.title: AWS Grew 39% and Booked a $578B Backlog. Amazon Spent $76B to Get There
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Amazon's third quarter showed AWS at its fastest growth in years and a backlog that more than doubled, while one quarter of capital spending ran at nearly three times the company's operating income.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • AWS revenue hit $46.0 billion in Q3, up 39%, with a $578 billion backlog that Andy Jassy says grew triple digits year over year.
  • Amazon spent $75.9 billion in cash capex in the quarter against $28.1 billion of operating income, and says 2027 spending will be meaningfully higher than 2026's roughly $220 billion.
  • Amazon intends to sell Trainium chips outside AWS starting late 2027, which would put it in direct competition with Nvidia for other people's data centers.

AWS is growing like it's 2021 again. Amazon's cloud unit brought in $46.0 billion in the third quarter, up 39% from a year ago, and posted $17.8 billion in operating income, Amazon said on its earnings call on Thursday, October 29.

The number that matters more is the backlog: $578 billion in contracted revenue that customers haven't been billed for yet. Jassy said on the call that it's growing triple digits year over year. That's the AI capacity deals showing up on paper.

The quarter in numbers

Per Amazon's call:

  • Net sales: $201.9 billion, up 12%
  • Operating income: $28.1 billion, a 13.9% margin and a company record
  • AWS: $46.0 billion revenue, $17.8 billion operating income
  • Advertising: $19.6 billion, up 12%, a clear slowdown
  • Q4 guidance: $240 to $247 billion in sales, $28.5 to $33.5 billion in operating income

The bill

Here's the part the backlog is paying for. Amazon spent $75.9 billion in cash capex in the quarter, nearly three times its operating income. Full-year 2026 capex is still tracking around $220 billion, and Jassy said 2027 will be meaningfully higher.

That gap doesn't close from retail. It closes only if the backlog converts to revenue on schedule and the chips, buildings and power contracts bought now still earn their keep in five years. Jassy called the backlog well diversified and said the largest capacity commitments are reserved well in advance, giving visibility into 2027 and 2028. That's a strong signal, but a backlog is a promise, not cash.

The ad slowdown is worth watching. Advertising was supposed to be the high-margin engine that helps fund the buildout, and its growth fell to 12% from 26% in the second quarter. Jassy blamed timing, mainly Prime Day moving into Q2, which he said took 850 basis points off Q3 ad growth, and expects growth to return to the high teens in Q4. The holiday season will settle that quickly.

Trainium leaves the building

The sleeper news: Amazon plans to sell Trainium chips outside AWS starting in late 2027. Jassy said strong Trainium demand has customers pushing Amazon to sell it outside AWS, though he added that the company is still weighing the trade-off.

Amazon has spent years pitching Trainium as a cheaper way to rent AI compute inside its own cloud. Selling it for other people's racks puts Amazon in the same market as Nvidia and AMD, not just Microsoft and Google.

For anyone buying cloud capacity, the practical read is simple. AWS is sold out enough to grow at 39% while spending this hard, so don't expect generous discounts on GPU or Trainium reservations next year.

item.title: SemiAnalysis Data Puts AMD's MI355X at Half B200's Cost for Kimi K3 Agents
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SemiAnalysis's InferenceX dashboard shows AMD's MI355X serving the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 on coding-agent traces for roughly half the cost per token of Nvidia's B200, and the reason is memory, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • On SemiAnalysis's agentic Kimi K3 test at FP4, MI355X costs $0.077 per million tokens at 100 tok/s per user versus $0.179 on B200, a gap of about 2.3x.
  • The gap is mostly throughput: SemiAnalysis says 2,304GB of HBM per MI355X server keeps the model on one box, while B200 servers have to spill across the network.
  • It's one model, one workload, interpolated data and SemiAnalysis's own price assumptions; buyers should test their own traffic before switching.

Seventy-seven cents versus a dollar seventy-nine. That's the per-ten-million-token cost SemiAnalysis's InferenceX dashboard shows for serving Kimi K3 on AMD's MI355X versus Nvidia's B200, at 100 tokens per second per user. SemiAnalysis highlighted the comparison in a post on X on Saturday, October 31, claiming up to 2x better performance per dollar for AMD.

Put another way: by the dashboard's own dollar figures, B200 costs about 2.3 times as much per token on this workload. Across the three interactivity levels on the page, the gap runs from roughly 1.9x to 2.3x, always in AMD's favor.

What the test actually measures

The setup matters more than the headline:

  • Model: Moonshot's Kimi K3, about 2.8 trillion parameters, at FP4
  • Workload: AgentX, which replays real coding-agent sessions where context grows every turn and much of each request hits cache
  • Cost basis: ownership TCO at hyperscaler volume, using SemiAnalysis's July pricing of $1.73 per B200 chip-hour and $1.50 for MI355X
  • Data: interpolated from benchmark runs, not measured at every point

So this is an inference benchmark for one very large model doing agent work. It says nothing about training, and nothing about smaller models that fit comfortably on any modern GPU.

Why AMD wins this one

Memory. SemiAnalysis says an MI355X server carries 2,304GB of HBM, enough to hold Kimi K3 and its growing caches on one box. A B200 server has under 1.5TB, so it has to split the model across servers and push traffic over much slower scale-out links. At 100 tok/s per user, MI355X pushes roughly twice the tokens per chip, and the cheaper chip-hour does the rest.

That's a real architectural advantage, not a benchmark trick. Trillion-parameter models running long agent sessions are exactly the workload that's growing fastest, and they punish anything that can't keep the whole model in one place.

The fine print

SemiAnalysis credits AMD's AITER kernel tuning and MonoKernel decode work for much of the result, which means the number reflects months of software work that won't automatically carry to your stack. The page's own percentage labels don't line up cleanly with its dollar figures, and the comparison doesn't include Nvidia's rack-scale GB200 or GB300 NVL72 systems, which attack the same memory problem by wiring 72 GPUs into one domain.

AMD also beat B300 on the same model in SemiAnalysis's comparison: $0.093 versus $0.166 per million tokens at about 109 tok/s per user, with B300 priced at $2.26 per chip-hour. If you're pricing out capacity for very large agent models in 2027, AMD belongs on the shortlist. Run your own traces before you sign anything.

item.title: OpenAI Lands $11B of a $30B Round and Cuts Its Target to $20B
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI has about $11 billion committed toward a round it pitched at $30 billion, and it has cut the goal to $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, with wealthy individuals expected to help fill the gap.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • OpenAI has roughly $11B committed toward a $30B round, per the Wall Street Journal.
  • The FT says the goal is now $20B at a $1.25T valuation, below the $1.4T OpenAI first sought.
  • Weak results from Google, Amazon and Intel fed a tech selloff that cooled big investors.
  • OpenAI wanted to close before Anthropic's expected mid-November IPO, according to Reuters.

OpenAI went looking for $30 billion and, so far, has found about $11 billion.

That's the core of a Wall Street Journal report on Friday, October 30, which says the round met a tepid response from some of the company's biggest prospective backers. The Financial Times reported the same day that OpenAI has cut the round's goal by $10 billion, to $20 billion, and that the first close is expected to come in below even that.

The valuation slipped too. The round prices OpenAI at $1.25 trillion, below the $1.4 trillion it was seeking when the raise was first reported in late September. OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, and no final figure for the first close had been announced as of Monday.

Why the money dried up

Timing did a lot of the damage. Disappointing quarterly results from Google, Amazon and Intel helped set off a tech selloff, according to the Journal. The Nasdaq fell 2.9% on Friday alone and finished 7.8% below its October 6 closing high, Reuters reported. Investors are asking harder questions about how all the AI spending pays off.

OpenAI's fallback plan says a lot. Per the Journal, it will spend the coming weeks pitching family offices and high-net-worth individuals, and the FT says a later offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total up to the $20 billion target.

A group of investors from the United Arab Emirates is expected to lead the round, according to the FT. Wealthy individuals are real money, but they aren't the strategic giants you'd expect to fill out a trillion-dollar round.

The Anthropic problem

The comparison investors keep making is with Anthropic. The Journal reports Anthropic's quarterly revenue more than doubled in the second quarter while it posted a small operating profit. Anthropic has filed to go public, and Reuters, citing the FT, says OpenAI wanted to close its round before Anthropic's expected market debut in mid-November because the two draw on a similar pool of investors.

OpenAI has clawed back some market share by cutting prices on its newest models, according to third-party data cited in the coverage. Cheaper models win customers, though, and they don't make a fundraising deck easier to sell.

A $20 billion raise at $1.25 trillion is still enormous. But OpenAI has now trimmed both the price and the size of this round in about a month because investors pushed back, and that matters more for its planned IPO than any single number in the round.

item.title: One robots.txt Rule Could Block AI Training at Four Big Labs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic plan to honor a single robots.txt opt-out for generative AI training, though Microsoft and Google won't support it until 2027 and live AI answers are still handled vendor by vendor.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic back one shared robots.txt signal to opt out of AI training.
  • Microsoft will honor the __usage_ai-training token from February 1, 2027; Google targets early 2027.
  • The signal targets training; live grounding for AI answers is still set vendor by vendor.
  • It's voluntary, unverifiable and doesn't touch content that's already been scraped.

Website owners currently write a separate robots.txt block for every AI company's training crawler. Four of the biggest labs now say one entry should be enough.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on Friday, October 30, that they'll support a shared opt-out signal that tells crawlers not to use a site's content to train generative AI models. The proposal is an individual Internet-Draft, draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal, submitted to the IETF's AI Preferences working group. It is not an official IETF standard.

The Kelley in the name is Kevin Kelley of Anthropic. In a post to the working group's mailing list, he wrote that "Anthropic has already started implementing support for this draft," while noting it will take time to add across the company's services.

What the rule looks like

Microsoft published the clearest details so far in a Bing blog post. To opt a whole site out of training, you'd add:

  • User-Agent: __usage_ai-training followed by Disallow: /
  • the same user agent with a path, like Disallow: /archive/, to opt out one section
  • a page-level ai-training:disallow value in a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header

One catch: a wildcard User-Agent: * group doesn't match the new token, so it needs its own block.

Microsoft says it will start honoring the new preferences as it crawls on February 1, 2027. After March 1, 2027, it will stop reading NoArchive and NoCache as AI preferences, so sites that relied on those tags need to publish the new ones.

Google's crawler documentation points to early 2027, and OpenAI says it aims to support the signal in the coming months, according to Search Engine Journal. By those timelines, none of the four fully supports it yet.

The part it doesn't fix

Training is only half the fight. When an AI assistant fetches your page to answer a question right now, that's grounding, and the shared signal is built for training.

Microsoft is handling grounding with its own page-level setting: ai-grounding:disallow blocks it, and ai-grounding:disallowextended allows grounding only in Microsoft-run products like Copilot and Microsoft 365. OpenAI plans similar controls, according to SiliconANGLE.

Google says a site that uses the shared opt-out without its own Google-Extended rule will be treated as if it had disallowed Google-Extended, which also covers grounding in Gemini Apps. That's still a different answer from each vendor for the traffic publishers care about most.

There's also no enforcement. Compliance is voluntary, nobody independently checks it, smaller labs aren't party to it, and nothing here claws back data already collected. Meta has said it supports the idea without committing to implement it.

What to do now: if you already block GPTBot, Google-Extended or ClaudeBot by name, keep those rules. Add the shared training rule in its own block once your crawlers' vendors confirm support, and audit any pages that rely on noarchive before Microsoft's March 1, 2027 cutoff.

item.title: Canada Buys Up to C$1.6B of Cohere, With Strings Attached
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Ottawa will take an equity stake of up to C$1.6 billion in Cohere's Series E, released in stages only if the AI lab stays Canadian, hires 1,000 technical staff and spends C$1.7 billion on domestic compute by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Canada will invest up to C$1.6B (about US$1.1B) in Cohere as part of a Series E targeting up to C$7B.
  • Money arrives in tranches tied to 1,000 Canadian tech jobs and C$1.7B of local compute by 2030.
  • Cohere has to keep its incorporation and headquarters in Canada, which Tech Times says gives Ottawa a veto over a foreign sale.
  • The round values Cohere at C$35.7B; Cohere hasn't said how much it has actually closed.

Canada is set to become a shareholder in its biggest AI lab. Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, October 29, that the federal government will invest up to C$1.6 billion in Toronto-based Cohere, taking an equity stake rather than handing out a grant.

The money comes as part of Cohere's Series E, which targets up to C$7 billion at a C$35.7 billion valuation. Germany's Schwarz Group leads the round. Bell Ventures and Bullhound Capital are new, and Nvidia, Inovia Capital and Prosperity7 are returning.

What Ottawa gets for its money

This isn't a blank check. The government will release its capital in stages, and each tranche depends on Cohere hitting commitments:

  • at least 1,000 high-paying Canadian technical jobs by 2030
  • at least C$1.7 billion spent on computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030
  • Canadian incorporation and headquarters, kept for good
  • research partnerships with Canadian institutions and pathways for students and new grads
  • continued work with the Canadian AI Safety Institute, plus regular progress reports

The headquarters clause is the real point. Tech Times argues that, combined with the staged payments, it gives Ottawa an ongoing veto over a sale to a U.S. or Chinese buyer without passing a law, though the agreement itself hasn't been published. Canada has watched a lot of its AI research talent and startups drift south. This is a bet that owning part of the company beats hoping it stays.

The caveats

Cohere announced a first close on October 29 but hasn't said how much of the C$7 billion is committed, so the headline round size is an aspiration for now. The company says annual recurring revenue at the end of the third quarter was up 165% year over year and its customer count grew 20-fold to 300, but it doesn't disclose the dollar figure behind the revenue growth.

Cohere's pitch is enterprise and government AI that customers can run on-premises or in fully air-gapped environments, and its 2026 combination with Germany's Aleph Alpha gave it a bigger European foothold. That control is a selling point for regulated buyers, and on-prem deployments are a cost burden for everyone else.

The deal landed the same week OpenAI reportedly fell far short of its own fundraising target. Private investors are getting pickier about AI valuations, and governments are stepping in where they see strategic value. Expect more of these sovereign-stake deals from countries that don't want to rent all their AI from California.

item.title: S&P Puts Meta's AA- Rating on Negative Outlook Over AI Spending
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: S&P Global kept Meta at AA- but moved its outlook to negative, projecting free operating cash flow deficits of $39 billion this year and $71 billion in 2027 as AI capex outruns the cash coming in.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • S&P revised Meta's outlook to negative from stable on Friday, October 30; the AA- rating is unchanged.
  • S&P expects free operating cash flow deficits of about $39B in 2026 and $71B in 2027.
  • Meta posted a $2.12B free cash flow deficit in Q3 and guided 2026 capex to $135B to $145B.
  • S&P says Meta has fewer ways than its peers to turn AI spending into revenue; Meta disagrees.

Meta spent more on data centers last quarter than its business generated in cash. On Friday, S&P Global Ratings noticed.

The agency moved Meta's outlook to negative from stable, citing what it called significant uncertainty around capital spending and free operating cash flow. The AA- rating stays where it is for now. A negative outlook is a warning, not a downgrade, but it tells bond investors which way S&P is leaning.

The numbers behind it

Meta's own third-quarter report did most of the work:

  • free cash flow came in at negative $2.12 billion
  • 2026 capex guidance sits at $135 billion to $145 billion
  • long-term debt reached about $81 billion at the end of September, up from roughly $59 billion at the end of 2025

S&P now expects free operating cash flow deficits of $39 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027, says the red ink could run past 2028, and expects Meta to fund its 2028 shortfall entirely with debt. It said leverage, about 0.1x in 2025, could climb above the 1.0x threshold for an AA- rating as soon as 2027, mainly because of leased data center capacity.

The sharper criticism

The line that should sting is about monetization. S&P said Meta's ability to make money from its AI investments is more limited than its peers', and that it's unclear when that revenue will outrun the rising costs. It also said it's less confident Meta will rein in spending the way S&P had expected.

Meta pushed back. "We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," a Meta spokesperson said, pointing to what the company called a "very strong credit profile."

That's the core difference with Microsoft, Google and Amazon. Each of them rents AI compute to customers through a cloud business. Meta is building for itself and has to earn it back through ads and newer AI products.

Meta has already moved to fund the build with equity, including the share sale and mandatory convertible it announced in October. That keeps leverage in check for a while, at the cost of diluting shareholders. Meta's stock fell about 15% in October and closed Friday at $614.99, below the $625 price of that share offering, according to Yahoo Finance.

An AA- company is not in trouble. But when the rating agencies start asking when the AI spending pays off, the question has moved from analyst notes to the cost of borrowing.

item.title: Fake Claude Code Update on Cursor's Marketplace Planted an SSH Backdoor
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: For about 11 hours on Thursday, Cursor's extension marketplace served a tampered build of Anthropic's Claude Code extension that added an attacker SSH key, tried to open a reverse tunnel and set persistence on developer machines.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Claude Code extension builds 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 on Cursor's marketplace were malicious between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on October 29, per Cursor.
  • The loader adds an SSH key labeled svc-telemetry, tries to tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225 and beacons host details, including the names of secret-looking env vars.
  • If you installed or auto-updated in that window, treat the machine as compromised and rotate credentials from a clean system.

Developers who let Cursor auto-update their extensions on Thursday may have pulled a backdoor dressed up as Anthropic's Claude Code. Cursor confirmed that a maliciously modified build of the extension sat in its extension marketplace from about 2:27 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. PT on October 29.

Cursor says Anthropic didn't build the bad versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. Nobody has said yet how the attacker got an update published under the legitimate anthropic.claude-code ID, and that's the part that should worry every editor marketplace.

What the loader does

OpenSourceMalware, which published the first analysis, found a 66-line loader inserted in front of the real extension code. It runs as soon as the extension loads. You don't have to open a Claude chat. It then:

  • Appends an attacker key labeled svc-telemetry to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  • Tries to enable SSH and open a reverse tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225
  • Beacons hostname, username, OS, Git email and the names (not values) of up to 40 env vars containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS or GCP
  • Persists via a LaunchAgent on macOS, a scheduled task on Windows or an @reboot crontab entry on Linux

Cursor says the SSH enable step would fail unless Cursor was running with admin rights. The key, the persistence and the beacon still land. Cursor also warns that uninstalling the extension may not be enough, because the payload drops standalone persistence scripts that keep running.

OpenSourceMalware and The Hacker News say no second-stage payload has been seen. That's less reassuring than it sounds: an env var list naming your AWS and CI tokens is a shopping list for whoever comes back through that tunnel.

What's confirmed and what isn't

Cursor puts the exposure at no more than 5,000 users, according to The Hacker News. Cursor pulled the build, shut its marketplace down as a precaution, rotated keys and worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline. The Hacker News reports it will contact affected users directly.

The accounts don't fully line up yet. Cursor's notice, revised Friday morning, names 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 on macOS and Windows; earlier reports named only 2.1.313. OpenSourceMalware says its sample came from Open VSX, while The Hacker News, after a correction, says there's no evidence the bad build reached Open VSX or Microsoft's marketplace. OpenSourceMalware also says its analysis doesn't show Anthropic's own release was compromised.

The Hacker News reports Anthropic has published 2.1.314 to Open VSX and Microsoft's marketplace. None of the reports so far carry a statement from the company.

What to do now

  1. Check whether 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 came from Cursor's marketplace during the window, and look for svc-telemetry in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
  2. Hunt for ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, a SysMon scheduled task, the files ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk, and traffic to 134.209.82[.]225 on ports 22 or 8099.
  3. Isolate any hit, remove the key and persistence, and consider a rebuild.
  4. Rotate cloud, CI and Git credentials reachable from that machine, using a different, trusted system.
  5. Update to 2.1.314 or later.

item.title: Attackers Poll WordPress Sites to Catch Updates Mid-Flight for RCE
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Wordfence blocked nearly 63,000 attempts in a day against a WordPress core race condition, fixed in 7.1.4 on Wednesday, that lets an anonymous visitor reach the installer while a full-package upgrade is unpacking.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • A race condition in WordPress core upgrades, affecting 4.7 through 7.1.3, can give an unauthenticated attacker code execution during the update window.
  • Wordfence says it blocked 62,969 attacks in 24 hours; reports so far describe attempts, not confirmed break-ins.
  • Update to 7.1.4 or your branch's backport, and deny web access to wp-content/upgrade/.

Attackers are camping on WordPress sites and waiting for them to update. Wordfence says it blocked 62,969 attempts in 24 hours against a core race condition that WordPress fixed in 7.1.4 on Wednesday, October 28.

The bug lives in full-package core upgrades. WordPress unpacked the new release, installer included, into a predictable folder under wp-content/upgrade/ that the web server would happily serve. Its cleanup routine also deleted the index.php that normally blocks directory listing.

That leaves a few seconds where a complete WordPress copy sits at a guessable, browsable path. Per Patchstack, an attacker who reaches it in time can run the installer against a database they control. Wordfence says that can progress to PHP code execution. No account and no user interaction needed.

Why the narrow window isn't comforting

Patchstack rates the attack complexity high and says it wouldn't call the bug practical to exploit. Fair enough for one site. But the window opens on every full core update, and Wordfence's Alex Thomas says two of the biggest attack sources polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours. That's exactly how you win a race: keep showing up.

There's an ugly irony, too. The fix is an update, and an update is exactly when you're exposed. That's a good reason to lock down the upgrade folder at the web server before you patch, not after.

None of the reports so far describe a confirmed break-in. The volume says attackers think it's worth trying anyway.

Affected and fixed versions

The Hacker News reports versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 are affected, and Patchstack traces the vulnerable code back to WordPress 2.8. Fixed releases include:

  • 7.1.4 for the current branch
  • 7.0.8 and 6.9.11
  • 6.8.12 and 6.7.11
  • Backports down to 4.7.39
  • 4.6 and older get nothing

Patchstack counts 22 vulnerabilities across 17 advisories in this release, so 21 more beyond this one. Most are stored XSS in blocks and the Interactivity API. WordPress also refreshed its bundled root certificates after the eMudhra revocation.

What to do now

  1. Confirm every site you run is on 7.1.4 or its branch's backport. Don't assume auto-updates fired.
