  2. Deny web requests to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server (nginx or Apache), not in a plugin, and make sure the folder isn't listable. Patchstack notes a PHP firewall can't stop this one: the staged copy loads WordPress from its own files, and the official zip ships no mu-plugins folder, so the site's firewall never runs.
  3. Search access logs for requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade/.
  4. Check for admin accounts, plugins or PHP files you don't recognize.

item.title: Binance Heist Pinned on North Korea's TraderTraitor as More Breaches Surface
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: TRM Labs and Chainalysis tie the roughly $6.3 billion Binance theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor unit, while Binance now says the attacker got in through more than one engineer's laptop.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • TRM Labs attributes the Binance theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor with high confidence, and Chainalysis ties it to the same group.
  • Binance says it found additional points of breach beyond the compromised DevOps laptop it first blamed.
  • Deposits are back, but withdrawals stay paused while Binance rebuilds its withdrawal service, with a restart targeted about 45 hours after its Friday update.
  • Binance says it will cover all losses; about $3 billion is frozen on-chain, per the exchange.

The biggest crypto theft on record now has a probable name attached. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs says, with high confidence, that North Korea's TraderTraitor unit drained Binance's hot wallets on Thursday, the same group the FBI blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

Chainalysis reached the same conclusion. CEO Jonathan Levin pointed to links with a previous hack, and on-chain investigator ZachXBT said funds from Binance and the earlier Bitget exploit were mixed together at one address.

Binance itself hasn't named a culprit. Neither has any government agency, so this is an analytics-firm attribution, not an official one yet.

It wasn't just one laptop

Early Friday UTC, Binance said a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have let an attacker reach a service container and push unauthorized withdrawals. Hours later it walked that back in part: its investigation has "uncovered additional points of breach," the company posted on X.

Co-CEO Richard Teng said the attacker "did not simply use one engineer's permissions" and that it wasn't a single "one-click" action. Binance still says it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak.

TRM's read of the chain lines up with that. It says the attacker likely took control of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure, used an EIP-7702 delegation to turn an Ethereum hot wallet into a sweeper, and moved funds out across ten chains. Prep started at least 36 hours earlier, funded with small Tornado Cash withdrawals and a test run.

Where the money stands

TRM puts the haul at about $6.36 billion at the time it was taken, roughly four times Bybit. Binance's own estimate is about $6.3 billion, with around $3 billion frozen by stablecoin issuers and others.

That still leaves billions with the attacker. TRM says it's holding over 420,000 ETH and about 18,270 BTC beyond any issuer's reach, splitting the Bitcoin through peel chains and dumping freezable USDT to market makers at a discount of more than 10%. If this follows the Bybit playbook, the next stop is bridges and OTC brokers.

Deposits are running normally again. Withdrawals stay paused during what Binance calls a security revamp of its withdrawal service, and the exchange says it's on track to restart them about 45 hours after its Friday update. It has promised a root-cause report and a technical post-mortem.

What to do now: if you hold funds on Binance, they're covered by the company's SAFU fund and its own money, per Binance, so don't rush to move assets through unofficial channels. Expect phishing that impersonates Binance "withdrawal restart" or "compensation" notices, and only trust announcements on Binance's own site or verified accounts.

item.title: OpenAI-Backed Thrive Holdings Agrees to Buy ADT for $15.3 Billion
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Thrive Holdings, the Thrive Capital spinout part-owned by OpenAI, will pay $10 a share in cash for ADT and says customer data policies won't change without permission.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Thrive Holdings will pay $10 per share in cash, about $7.6B in equity and $15.3B including debt, a 45.6% premium.
  • Apollo-managed funds are the sole financing; a go-shop runs to November 28 and the deal should close in Q1 2027.
  • ADT says its data and privacy policies stay the same and no new data sharing will happen without customer permission.

One of the biggest names in home alarms is about to belong to a company built around putting OpenAI's models into old-line businesses. ADT agreed on Thursday, October 29, to be acquired by Thrive Holdings for $10 a share in cash.

That values ADT's equity at about $7.6 billion and the whole company, debt included, at $15.3 billion. The price is a 45.6% premium to ADT's unaffected close of $6.87 on October 27, according to ADT's announcement.

Who's buying

Thrive Holdings spun out of Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital, one of OpenAI's major investors. OpenAI is an investor and partner, and sends its own engineers to work inside Thrive's companies. Until now that meant accounting firms (Current) and IT services shops (Shield), more than 75 businesses in all. ADT is a much bigger and much more consumer-facing bet.

Deal terms

  • Financing: funds managed by Apollo affiliates, with no financing condition
  • Go-shop: ADT can seek better offers until November 28, with a possible 10-day extension
  • Approvals: ADT stockholders and U.S. antitrust review
  • Expected close: first quarter of 2027

Neither side named a single AI product it plans to build. Thrive says its engineers will work with ADT's staff to find where technology can improve products and services, and that ADT becomes the base of its smart home security business.

The data question

That vagueness is why the privacy language matters. A security company holds camera feeds, alarm histories, door codes and the daily routines of millions of households. ADT's release says its data and privacy policies "will remain unchanged, and no new data sharing will occur without customer permission."

That's a clear commitment, and it's on the record. The obvious follow-up is what "permission" looks like once the AI features arrive: a buried checkbox in a terms update, or a real opt-in. ADT customers should watch their next policy notice closely.

item.title: Intel Beats on Q3, Then Guides Q4 Low on PCs, Memory and Its Israel Fab
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Intel's data center sales jumped 78% last quarter, but a $15B to $16B fourth-quarter forecast, blamed on a shrinking PC market, memory prices and the Kiryat Gat shutdown, sent the stock sharply lower after hours.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Q3 revenue was about $16.5B, up 21%, with data center and AI up 78% to $7.3B and PC chips down 5% to $8.1B.
  • Q4 guidance of $15B to $16B and 25 cents adjusted EPS came in well below the roughly $17B and 43 cents analysts wanted.
  • Intel puts the cost of the October Fab 28 shutdown in Israel at about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters.

Intel had a good quarter and a bad forecast, and the forecast won. Shares fell more than 20% in after-hours trading on Thursday, by The Next Web's count, after the company said fourth-quarter revenue would land between $15 billion and $16 billion.

Analysts had been looking for about $17 billion. Intel's adjusted EPS guide of 25 cents was well short of the 43 cents expected.

The quarter itself was fine

Third-quarter revenue came in around $16.5 billion, up 21% from a year earlier, and adjusted EPS of 52 cents beat estimates, according to Ynet. The split tells the real story:

  • Data center and AI: up 78% to $7.3 billion
  • Client (PC) chips: down 5% to $8.1 billion

Server demand is doing what everyone hoped. PCs are going the other way.

Three things hit the outlook

First, PCs. Intel now expects the PC market to shrink 12% this year and another 10% in 2027, per The Next Web. Second, memory. With DRAM prices climbing, PC makers are building fewer machines. CEO Lip-Bu Tan told Bloomberg that memory pricing "went up a lot" and predicted it will be "a very severe issue to all of us" in 2027.

Third, Israel. The gas explosion at Fab 28 in Kiryat Gat on October 14 killed two workers and halted production. CFO David Zinsner put the cost at about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters and said Intel expects to start ramping the plant back up by the end of this week.

That last number deserves a pause. It's the first time Intel has put a figure on the accident, and it's large enough on its own to explain a good chunk of the gap to consensus.

Why the drop was so steep

The stock had more than doubled this year on the 18A ramp in Arizona and hopes for outside foundry customers. A forecast this far below expectations punctures that story fast. Intel's own data center growth shows the AI demand is real. Its PC business, which is still about half of revenue, is now exposed to a memory crunch it doesn't control.

Watch whether Intel names a major external 14A customer. That's the news that could reset the narrative; another quarter of strong servers probably won't.

item.title: Mistral Releases Large 4 Weights, but Selling It as an API Needs a License
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Mistral put the weights of its 1-trillion-parameter Large 4 on Hugging Face under a modified MIT license that is free for internal use and requires a separate deal for anyone serving it as a model service.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Mistral Large 4 is a 1T-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 50B active per token, now downloadable in FP8, NVFP4 and GGUF.
  • The license is free for internal and commercial use, except that Model-as-a-Service operators need a separate commercial license.
  • The headline benchmark wins are Mistral's own numbers; running the full model still takes a multi-GPU server.

Mistral delivered on its promise. The weights for Mistral Large 4, the 1-trillion-parameter model it previewed earlier this month, landed on Hugging Face on Thursday, October 29.

It's a mixture-of-experts model: 128 experts, four routed plus one shared per token, and roughly 50 billion parameters active at a time. Mistral's naming says 52B active; Hugging Face's launch post says 49B. Either way, you pay the inference cost of a mid-size model while storing a giant one. Hugging Face lists a 1M-token context, though the serving recipes default to 131K.

What you can download

  • mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B in FP8
  • an NVFP4 checkpoint for Blackwell GPUs
  • GGUF quants from ggml-org and Unsloth, down to 2-bit
  • day-one support in vLLM, SGLang, Transformers and llama.cpp

The FP8 recipe on Hugging Face runs on eight H200s. The 2-bit quants squeeze onto a single 512 GB Apple Silicon Ultra machine. This is not a laptop model.

The license catch

Mistral calls it the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, a modified MIT. Internal use is free, including commercial use. The exception is spelled out in section 2: any company that "operates a Model as a Service business" must sign a separate commercial license before using the model for any commercial purpose. The license defines that as giving a third party access to the model for inference or post-training.

So enterprises can self-host it behind the firewall without a call to Paris. Inference providers can't resell it without one. That's a reasonable line for a company that also sells the same model through its own API at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output.

About those benchmarks

Mistral says three more weeks of reinforcement learning after the preview lifted its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score from 28% to 41%, with fewer output tokens. It also claims 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0, the top open-weight score, and a tie with GLM-5.3 on Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index while using about half the tokens. All of those are Mistral's own figures, and Hugging Face's post still quotes the older preview numbers in places, which tells you how fresh this all is.

The cyber pitch is louder. Mistral reports 51% on Artificial Analysis's Cyber Index and a 96.6% average refusal rate on malicious cyber prompts. The preview post went further, claiming closed rivals score near zero on a reproduce-and-patch test only because they refuse the task. That's a benchmark measuring willingness as much as skill, and it's worth reading that way.

A full technical report is still to come. A cyber-tuned variant is limited to design partners and isn't part of the open release.

item.title: Drupal Commerce Access Bypass Is Exploited; Audit Your Orders After Patching
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Drupal rates the Commerce Core flaw CVE-2026-118539 highly critical and says it's under active attack, with fixes in 3.3.13 and 8.x-2.41 and an instruction to check orders for tampering.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Commerce Core before 2.41 and 3.x before 3.3.13 fail to protect certain routes and entity fields (SA-CONTRIB-2026-254, CVE-2026-118539).
  • Drupal says it's being exploited and that it may financially hit vendors; no attackers or victims have been named.
  • Update to 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41, then audit orders, coupons and product variations for changes you didn't make.

Drupal's security team shipped a fix for Commerce Core on Wednesday, October 28, and attached a line you don't often see in a contrib advisory: sites should audit their orders, because the bug is already being exploited.

The advisory, SA-CONTRIB-2026-254 (CVE-2026-118539), says the module "doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields." Drupal scores it Highly critical, 21 out of 25 on its own scale, and says it "may financially impact the vendor." Commerce runs on more than 42,000 sites, per BleepingComputer's count from drupal.org.

Affected and fixed versions

  • Affected: Commerce Core before 2.41, and 3.x before 3.3.13
  • Fixed: Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 and 3.3.13

What an attacker can change

Drupal hasn't published a technical breakdown. Ostorlab worked one out from the fix's tests, and the list is mostly about money and ownership. According to its analysis, the patch now locks down fields such as an order's state, total_price, adjustments and item unit_price, a variation's product_id, and a coupon's promotion_id.

In practice that means a customer could edit their own cart's prices or state through JSON:API or REST, and a user with limited commerce permissions could move another vendor's variation onto their own product or reassign coupons. The coupon autocomplete route could also list coupon codes.

There's a disagreement worth knowing about. Drupal's risk vector says no authentication is needed. Ostorlab says the takeover paths need at least a customer account or a limited commerce permission. On a store where anyone can sign up, that difference is small.

Nobody has said who is exploiting it or how many shops were hit, and no indicators have been published. Neither Drupal nor the researchers say card data or customer records were read.

What to do now

  1. Update with composer require 'drupal/commerce:^3.3.13' --with-all-dependencies (or ^2.41 on the 2.x line), then run drush cr
  2. Re-apply any custom patches you carry against the module
  3. Audit recent orders for totals, adjustments or states that don't match what was paid
  4. Check coupons whose promotion changed and variations that moved to another product
  5. Review JSON:API and REST writes to commerce entities from low-privilege accounts

Turning off JSON:API cuts down the write paths but doesn't cover the autocomplete and delete routes, so it's a stopgap, not a fix.

item.title: GitLab's CVSS 10 Regex Bug Is Exploited, and Alpine Shows Patching Wasn't Enough
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added GitLab's CVE-2026-97229 to its exploited list after attackers went after Alpine Linux's instance, which stayed vulnerable through two upgrades because the real fix lives in Ruby.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • CISA added CVE-2026-97229, an unauthenticated RCE in GitLab's CI/CD regex compiler (CVSS 10.0), to its exploited list on Thursday.
  • Alpine Linux's GitLab was attacked on October 21 and stayed exploitable after upgrading, because its image ran stock Ruby without the Onigmo fix.
  • Official GitLab packages at 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 are fixed; custom builds also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9.

Upgrading GitLab didn't save Alpine Linux. The distro bumped its self-hosted instance twice after GitLab patched CVE-2026-97229, and an attacker who had registered an ordinary account still spent a week throwing crafted CI configurations at it.

On Thursday, October 29, CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Federal agencies have until Sunday to deal with it. Everyone else should treat that as their deadline too.

What the bug does

CVE-2026-97229 is an integer overflow in the regular expression compiler GitLab uses to evaluate CI/CD configuration. GitLab's October 12 patch release scores it 10.0 and says it could let an unauthenticated user run arbitrary code on the server with a specially crafted regex. A researcher using the HackerOne handle joaxcar reported it.

Affected and fixed versions of GitLab CE and EE:

  • 19.2 before 19.2.8
  • 19.3 before 19.3.5
  • 19.4 before 19.4.2

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched. GitLab also published six threat detections for self-managed customers, keyed on things like native worker crashes in Onigmo and oversized non-ASCII regexes in CI lint requests.

Why Alpine was still exposed

The catch is in Alpine's incident write-up. The underlying flaw sits in Onigmo, Ruby's built-in regex engine, and GitLab's fix is a Ruby patch that it applies only inside its official packages. Alpine builds its own GitLab container on standard Ruby, so it never got that patch.

Alpine's timeline makes the gap plain:

  • Oct 13: Alpine upgrades to 19.3.4 instead of the fixed 19.3.5 by mistake
  • Oct 20: attacker registers an account and starts probing
  • Oct 21: main attack, eight worker crashes, 502s and failed CI jobs
  • Oct 22: upgrade to 19.3.6, still vulnerable on stock Ruby
  • Oct 23: attacker's account blocked; upstream Ruby ships the fix
  • Oct 27: GitLab closed to all but developers and builders, rebuild starts
  • Oct 28: rebuild done, all passwords reset, secret keys replaced

Alpine says it found no evidence the attacker's code ran, and its signing keys never lived on the GitLab server. It verified aports, packages and the October 21 point releases against records outside GitLab. It also admits it can't rule out execution: a clean exploit leaves no crash, some logs from October 20 and 21 are gone, and it wasn't logging outbound connections. That's an honest write-up, and a useful one.

What to do now: if you run GitLab from the official Omnibus or Helm packages, get to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 or later and you're covered. If you build GitLab yourself, ship it in a container you made, or run it on a distro Ruby, check the Ruby version too: the fix is in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9. Anything else that compiles regexes from untrusted input on an unpatched Ruby has the same exposure.

Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 internet-facing GitLab CE instances, per BleepingComputer. The ones most likely to be missed are exactly the hand-built ones that looked patched on paper.

item.title: Binance Blames Hacked Engineer Laptop, Puts Theft at About $6.3 Billion
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Binance's first findings say an attacker used a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop to reach a service container and push unauthorized withdrawals, with no sign of a leaked wallet key and an estimated total impact of around $6.3 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Binance's initial findings say a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop let an attacker into a service container that submitted unauthorized withdrawals.
  • Its own estimate of the total impact is around $6.3 billion, with about $3 billion frozen onchain so far.
  • No private key leak found, per Binance, which points at abuse of its signing pipeline rather than stolen keys.
  • As of that update, deposits and withdrawals were suspended; ignore anyone offering early access to your funds.

A compromised laptop is the first explanation Binance has offered for the largest crypto theft on record. In a post on its official X account early Friday UTC, the exchange said its initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop gave an attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

Binance also put a number on it for the first time. It estimates the total impact at around $6.3 billion, above the roughly $5.8 billion that outside trackers had been citing and Chainalysis's estimate of about $5.9 billion, per Cointelegraph's live coverage.

No leaked key, says Binance

The exchange said it has found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. That matters because Thursday's main sweep ran through an EIP-7702 delegation on a hot wallet, and that kind of transaction needs a valid signature from the wallet's key.

Put the two together and the likely story is that the attacker never held the key. They got inside the machinery that asks for signatures and had it approve withdrawals on their behalf. Blockaid floated exactly that theory hours earlier, suspecting a compromise of signing infrastructure rather than a stolen key. Binance hasn't spelled it out, and it calls these findings preliminary.

If it holds, it's an uncomfortable lesson for every exchange. Cold storage and key ceremonies don't help much when an engineer's endpoint can reach a container that's trusted to request hot-wallet signatures.

Where the money stands

Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen onchain with help from partners, and it has revoked the affected address authorization, according to Bitcoin.com. Frozen isn't the same as recovered. First Digital said it froze FDUSD tied to the attack, adding to earlier freezes by Tether, Circle, Ripple and others.

The company repeated that losses will be covered from its SAFU fund and company funds. As of that update, deposits and withdrawals were suspended. Co-CEO Yi He said withdrawals will come back once the security scan is complete, and Binance has promised a proof-of-reserves update and a full technical post-mortem. Nobody has been named as the attacker.

What to do now: if you hold funds on Binance, there's nothing to do but wait for the reopening notice on Binance's own channels. Treat any message offering early withdrawals or account recovery as a scam. If you run exchange or treasury infrastructure, check which engineer endpoints can reach anything that requests signatures, and whether a single laptop could do it alone.

Update: Binance later said its investigation found additional points of breach beyond the laptop, and analytics firms now tie the theft to North Korea. Read the latest.

item.title: Binance Says It Will Cover All Hack Losses, Freezes Deposits and Withdrawals
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Binance now says in its own name that it will absorb every loss from Thursday's hot-wallet drain, but it also reversed the partial reopening and suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it reports about $3 billion of the stolen assets frozen.
item.content:encoded:
Binance has put the promise in writing. In a post on its official X account early Friday UTC, the exchange said: "Binance will cover all losses. As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement." Co-founder Yi He said the same in a separate statement: Binance will cover all hacking losses.

That closes the gap we flagged in our first report. Until now the only person saying users would be made whole was Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company and was speaking as a shareholder. Now it's the company itself.

The catch is access. Late Thursday, Binance had reopened BTC, ETH and Ethereum-based USDT and USDC withdrawals while other networks stayed paused. The new statement shuts everything, deposits included, with no date for reopening. Binance says it will resume once the issue is fully resolved and that it will publish a detailed report on the cause and timeline when its investigation ends.

On the recovery side, Binance said Thursday that $2.54 billion of the affected assets had been frozen, then updated that to about $3 billion verified, adding that it will only share confirmed figures. Tether froze roughly $1.57 billion in USDT and Circle more than $800 million in USDC, per their CEOs.

Yi He also credited Ripple with freezing about $200 million and World Liberty Financial, with custodian BitGo, with about $27 million in stablecoins. Binance has still not published a total loss figure. Outside estimates range from Blockaid's $3.3 billion in suspicious outflows to as much as $5.8 billion from Coinbase's Conor Grogan, and those aren't confirmed losses.

What's still unknown matters more than what's new. Nobody has attributed the theft, and Binance hasn't explained how an attacker got a signature from a hot-wallet key. The roughly 195,000 ETH that moved can't be frozen the way stablecoins can, so whatever Binance ends up covering will lean heavily on that ETH.

If you hold funds on Binance, nothing you do right now gets them out, so don't fall for anyone offering to. Binance itself warned users to watch for scams, and a frozen exchange is prime bait for fake support accounts and phishing sites promising early withdrawals. Wait for the reopening notice on Binance's own channels, and check that any link you click actually goes to binance.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell Hits Palo Alto Firewalls: 24 Rooted via Exposed Admin Pages
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Palo Alto Networks confirms attackers are exploiting the PHP2Shell flaws against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces, and Dream Security says one campaign chained them with the Fragnesia kernel bug to get root on 24 firewalls.
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • Attackers are exploiting PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet.
  • Dream Security says 24 of 240 targeted firewalls were rooted by chaining the bugs with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw.
  • Fixed builds are out for nearly every supported branch. Panorama is affected; Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not.
  • Take the management interface off the internet, patch, then hunt for compromise.

The PHP2Shell bugs have found the worst possible home: firewall admin pages. Palo Alto Networks updated its advisory for CVE-2026-109618 on October 29 to say active exploitation has been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet, and Unit 42 says it has verified a campaign that turned that access into root.

That campaign was first written up by Dream Security. According to Dream, the operators found about 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls, narrowed the list to 240 targets in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, and rooted 24 of them.

They got in through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both 9.2 under CVSS 4.0), then escalated with Fragnesia, the Linux kernel privilege escalation tracked as CVE-2026-46300. A 25th system, an internal firewall management server, fell later through a reverse SSH tunnel.

What the attackers did with root

On 22 of the 24 rooted boxes, the attackers planted a webshell and stopped there. The other two are the scary part.

Dream describes the attackers pivoting to domain controllers and GlobalProtect, decrypting an LDAP service account password from the management server, enumerating Active Directory and pulling private keys off the firewall filesystem. Attempts at SAML key extraction and backdoor accounts were seen, but Dream couldn't confirm they worked.

Attribution is soft. Dream says multiple indicators point to a China-nexus operation but names no group, and it reports that Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-UNK-1280, a Chinese-speaking actor working in UTC+8. Palo Alto says only about 0.02% of its installed base had an internet-facing management interface and was hit, and that each of those customers has been contacted.

Fixed builds

Fixes are out for nearly every supported branch. These are the top-of-branch targets, with hotfixes for older maintenance trains listed in the advisory:

  • 12.2.4-h1
  • 12.1.10-h3
  • 11.2.16-h1
  • 11.1.16-h4
  • 10.2.18-h13

As of Thursday, the only one still pending was 11.1.7-h12, due October 30. Panorama is affected too. Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not.

What to do now

It's worth saying plainly: this whole chain depends on a management interface that anyone on the internet can reach. Palo Alto has been telling customers to lock that down for years, and this is the latest PAN-OS management bug to punish the people who didn't.

  1. Pull internet access to the management interface and restrict it to trusted internal IPs or a jump box.
  2. Patch PAN-OS and Panorama to a fixed build.
  3. If your admin page was exposed at any point since the flaws were disclosed on October 21, hunt for compromise before you trust a clean upgrade.

Dream's indicators include:

  • A webshell at /unauth/php/change_password.php
  • A persistence directory at /usr/local/lib/.panops/
  • Unexpected systemd services and rc.local boot hooks
  • Outbound reverse SSH tunnels

If you find any of it, assume the device's keys and any service account credentials it held are burned, and rotate them.

item.title: Binance Hot Wallets Drained of $3 Billion or More in Suspected Key Compromise
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An EIP-7702 delegation signed with a Binance hot-wallet key let an attacker sweep 167,000 ETH and more than $1.6 billion in USDT in a single transaction, Tether and Circle froze roughly $2 billion in flight, and if the tallies hold this is the largest crypto theft on record.
item.content:encoded:
At 20:24 UTC on Thursday a single transaction moved 167,464 ETH and 63 other tokens, including about $1.6 billion in USDT, out of the Binance hot wallet labelled Binance 14. Two minutes later another 28,000 ETH left Binance 16. Fifteen minutes after that, 780 million USDC left Hot Wallet 34.

By 21:04 the sweeps had stopped and analysts were arguing about whether the total was $2.8 billion, $3.3 billion or $3.55 billion. Binance hasn't offered a number. CoinDesk's high-end estimate runs to $5.7 billion across chains, though that includes movements nobody has firmly tied to the attacker.

Whatever the final figure, it's at least double Bybit's $1.46 billion from February 2025, which the FBI pinned on North Korea and which was, until Thursday, the largest crypto theft ever. Nobody has attributed this one. Binance says it's investigating a potential security issue. One analyst has said it looks like Lazarus. That's a guess so far.

The mechanism is the detail that matters. Four minutes before the sweep, a transaction set an EIP-7702 delegation on Binance 14, pointing the wallet at a contract the attacker had deployed at 15:59 UTC from an address funded with 0.1 ETH out of Tornado Cash the day before.

EIP-7702 has been live since Ethereum's Pectra upgrade in May 2025. It lets an ordinary wallet temporarily act like a smart contract, and it requires a signature from that wallet's private key.

There is no version of this where a bug in a contract did it. Someone signed with the Binance 14 key, and the contract they delegated to only accepts calls from the Tornado-funded address. One researcher counted fifty delegations in the single transaction.

The stablecoin issuers moved fast. Paolo Ardoino said Tether froze about $1.57 billion in USDT. Jeremy Allaire said Circle froze more than $800 million in USDC.

On-chain, about $975 million USDT and $823 million USDC are visibly blacklisted at the main receiving address, so the verifiable frozen total is closer to $1.8 billion than the $2.4 billion implied by the two CEOs' posts. The ETH is a different story. Nobody can freeze 195,000 ETH, and the attacker had already started moving it to fresh addresses by 20:39.

Changpeng Zhao posted at 21:15 UTC: 'User funds are safe! It does look like a hack on Binance.' Co-founder Yi He added SAFU, the emergency fund Binance set up in 2018 and used to cover a 7,000 BTC hot-wallet theft in 2019. Binance's official statement nine minutes later was softer, acknowledging reports of a potential security issue and saying user funds are completely safe.

Spokesperson Ross O'Leary told TechCrunch withdrawals were temporarily suspended on multiple networks as a precaution. As of 23:21 UTC, BTC, ETH and Ethereum-based USDT and USDC withdrawals were open again. Solana, XRP and several other networks were still paused, which Binance described as wallet maintenance.

Two things don't sit right. 'User funds are safe' and 'we haven't confirmed a hack' are being said in the same hour by the same company, and a $3 billion hole is roughly the size of the entire SAFU fund depending on the day's prices.

Zhao, who no longer runs the exchange, said he expects all user funds to be fully covered. That's an expectation from a shareholder, not a commitment from the company. Until Binance publishes a loss figure and says in its own words that it will absorb it, the reassurance is doing a lot of work.

BNB dropped about 6%. The broader market sold off overnight. If you hold assets on Binance, the practical question isn't whether your balance shows correctly, it's whether you can withdraw it on the network you need, and for several networks the answer right now is no.

item.title: Polymarket Halts Trading After a Vendor Monitoring Script Drained About $2.7M
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A third-party real-user-monitoring script loaded on polymarket.com was swapped for a drainer that sold positions and pushed funds out through Polymarket's own relayer, hitting roughly 700 wallets before the exchange went cancel-only for about an hour.
item.content:encoded:
Polymarket went into cancel-only mode at 18:05 UTC on Thursday, which is the polite way of saying it pulled the plug while users watched their positions get sold out from under them.

By the time trading resumed around 19:00 UTC, on-chain trackers had counted roughly $2.7 million gone from about 700 wallets. Polymarket's statement was short: one of its third-party providers was compromised, and the matter has been referred to law enforcement. It did not name the provider.

Researchers did. Hudson Rock and others traced the drainer to a JavaScript file served from DebugBear's CDN, the real-user-monitoring embed Polymarket loaded on its homepage. DebugBear posted on X that it was impacted by an ongoing security incident and told customers to remove its embed code.

A Polymarket production build timestamped 17:59 UTC carried the note 'remove debugbear rum script.' Neither company has published a post-mortem, so the exact point of compromise on DebugBear's side is still their story to tell.

The mechanism is what makes this worth reading even if you've never touched a prediction market. The script didn't steal keys. It didn't need to. It read local storage and React state to find the live trading client, then sent properly signed EIP-712 batches through Polymarket's own relayer to unwrap balances and route them to a hard-coded attacker address.

For accounts that log in by email, it placed fill-and-kill sells at 97% of market, then 50%, then the minimum tick, dumping whatever it could into whoever was on the other side. Arkham tracked the attacker wallet swapping USDC.e for POL and holding about $2.65 million in it afterward. Everything happened on Polygon.

Polymarket's U.S. platform, the CFTC-regulated one, wasn't touched, according to a person familiar who spoke to CNBC. The halt covered the international site only. Polymarket says every affected trader will be fully reimbursed. No mechanism or timeline for that yet.

This is the second time this year a vendor script on Polymarket's frontend has turned into a drainer. In June it was a different third party. A page that signs transactions on behalf of logged-in users cannot safely load arbitrary JavaScript from a vendor's CDN, and a monitoring script is arbitrary JavaScript with full DOM access.

Subresource integrity doesn't help when the vendor is expected to update the file. A content security policy that limits what the script can talk to would have made the exfiltration harder, but the sells went through Polymarket's legitimate relayer, so even that is a partial answer.

The fix that actually works is boring: no third-party scripts on any page where a session can move money. Serve performance monitoring from your own origin or don't serve it at all. Polymarket learned that in June and loaded another one anyway.

item.title: Anthropic's Unreleased Claude Built Working Exploits for Five Major Platforms
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team reports five end-to-end exploit chains from an internal model with little human involvement, including 62 Chrome CVEs and a zero-click Linux root, but the public CVE records don't all line up with the write-up.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-two Chrome CVEs, all rated high or critical, thirteen of them sandbox escapes. That's the count Anthropic's Frontier Red Team says one unreleased internal model turned in, and it's the least dramatic part of the October 27 write-up. The post describes five full exploit chains the model built across Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux, each after what Anthropic calls initial prompting and with little human involvement.

The Chrome chain is a one-click remote code execution on macOS that strings together V8 heap corruption, a V8 sandbox escape with an ASLR defeat, a CacheStorage race and a FedCM use-after-free to run code outside the renderer sandbox. Google fixed the bugs in Chrome 156, released October 20, and credits Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude, on specific entries. The Safari chain breaks same-origin policy through a JavaScriptCore use-after-free, a Gigacage bypass and an IPC flaw, enough to read another site's cookies and authenticated responses, and Apple shipped the fix in iOS 26.5.2 crediting Milad Nasr and Nicholas Carlini with Claude.

The Linux one is the scary one. A race-condition use-after-free in the multipath TCP stack, chained with a KASLR leak, gives zero-click remote root on any box with an MPTCP listener. Anthropic tied it to CVE-2026-98432, a 9.8 fixed upstream October 15 and backported to stable. The Android chain extracts photos from a locked Pixel over USB by defeating three separate checks. The Windows chain is a kernel denial of service in QUIC handling.

Here's where it gets less tidy. The Hacker News went and checked the public records. The CVE-2026-98432 entry describes an IPv4 TCP fix, not multipath TCP, and the only thing connecting it to Anthropic's chain is Anthropic's post. The Windows bug, CVE-2026-33096, was patched in April, is described by Microsoft as an HTTP.sys issue rated 7.5, and credits no finder at all.

The Android fix has no public record anyone has found. None of that means the work didn't happen. It does mean the vendors' paper trail and Anthropic's narrative are not the same document, and the post doesn't say what a human did at each step.

Anthropic isn't naming the model or releasing it, and it doesn't explain why beyond the obvious. It says the reports went through its standard disclosure policy, 90 days to patch and 45 more before details, and it's expanding its Cyber Verification Program for defenders.

Google said something very similar a day later when it gated Gemini 4 Carbon behind a vetted-defender program. Two labs in two days telling you their best cyber models are too capable to ship broadly is either a coordinated marketing beat or a real inflection. It can be both.

What should change on your end is simpler than the debate. If a model can produce a working MPTCP root chain from a prompt, then every piece of code you expose to the network is now cheaper to attack than it was a month ago, and the only lever you control is whether you scan it first.

Anthropic's advice is to run your own code through these tools before someone else does. That's self-serving. It's also correct.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Goes to Vetted Cyber Defenders First, Everyone Else Waits
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google's new frontier model leads its own exploit-finding and patching benchmarks, ships two weeks after Argon at the same $2 and $10 per million tokens, and is gated behind the Fairwind program because Google says the offensive capability is real.
item.content:encoded:
Two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon went generally available, Google has a new top model, and you can't use it. Gemini 4 Carbon launched October 28 to a subset of cyber defenders, with access widening through what Google calls the Fairwind Program before developers, businesses and consumers get it at some unspecified later point. The stated reason is that the model is good enough at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities that Google wants guardrails and government pre-release testing done first.

The benchmarks Google chose to lead with tell you what the model is for. SEC-bench Pro, which measures vulnerability discovery, at 88.2%. ExploitGym, which measures turning a bug into a working exploit, at 54.8%. CWE-bench, for patching, at 71%. Google says Carbon leads every competing model on all three.

These are Google's own evaluations on Google's chosen benchmarks, so treat the ranking claim the way you'd treat any vendor leaderboard. But the shape of it is clear: this is a model built to do security work end to end, including the offensive half.

The more interesting claims come from the people who've used it. Google says the Chrome team found Carbon generated high-quality patches more than ten times as often as another lab's large frontier model, and that Wiz has it leading on web penetration testing benchmarks. Neither quote is independently verifiable yet, and the Chrome comparison doesn't name the other model, but if you're the team that just took 62 CVE reports from Anthropic's unreleased research model, you'd want the patching side to be fast too.

The rest of the release notes are about reliability rather than raw capability. Unsupported claims cut roughly in half versus Argon. Prompt injection attack success rate on Google's benchmark down from 0.7% to 0.0%. A measure Google calls cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 reduced to zero.

That last one is worth noticing. The fact that it's a reported metric at all means models gaming the task harness was a real problem on the previous generation, and Google is now treating it as something to fix and publish.

Pricing is unchanged from Argon's introductory rate: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, rising to $4 and $20 after the intro period, with cached input at 95% off. So the gate on Carbon is access, not cost. For defenders inside the program, that's a cheap way to run a frontier exploit-finder across your own codebase. For everyone else, Argon is what you get.

The staged rollout is the right call and also a convenient one. It lets Google say the model is too capable for general release while still shipping it to the customers who'll pay the most for exactly that capability.

Anthropic made the same choice last week with a model it hasn't named at all. The pattern is now set: the best cyber models go to a short list first, and the short list is where the money is.

item.title: Alphabet Burns $9 Billion in a Quarter, Stock Drops 10% Despite Cloud Doubling
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Alphabet's Q3 was its first top-and-bottom-line miss in nearly four years, free cash flow went to negative $9.1 billion on capex and a TPU inventory build, and Microsoft's Azure beat the same evening made the contrast painful.
item.content:encoded:
Revenue up 25%. Google Cloud up 103%. A half-trillion-dollar run rate, per Sundar Pichai. And the stock fell around 10% after hours. Alphabet's third quarter is a lesson in what investors are actually grading right now, and it isn't growth.

Start with the number that did the damage. Free cash flow for the quarter was negative $9.1 billion. Operating cash flow came in at $42.3 billion, but Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on property and equipment, and on the call management pointed to two more drags: a $5.2 billion cash payment on a 2018 European Commission fine and a build-up of inventory for TPU system sales.

Inventory on the balance sheet went from $2.4 billion at year-end to $13.3 billion. Management says all of it is tied to committed contracts. That's probably true. It's also an awful lot of silicon sitting in a warehouse while the cash is already out the door.

The headline miss was modest. Revenue of $127.6 billion against roughly $128.2 billion expected, per CNBC, and adjusted earnings of $2.67 a share against $3.02. GAAP diluted EPS was $2.12, dragged by an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities. Nearly four years without a miss on either line is a long streak, and breaking it on the same night the free cash flow line went red is a bad combination.

Then there's capex guidance, which is where the 10% really came from. Alphabet held its 2026 range at $195 billion to $205 billion and said 2027 will increase significantly. No number.

The market has been willing to fund the AI build-out as long as the spend had a visible ceiling. Telling investors the ceiling is higher but declining to say how much higher is the kind of thing that gets punished when free cash flow is already negative.

Microsoft reported the same evening and got the opposite reaction. Revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, Azure growth of 48% in constant currency against its own 44% to 45% guide, and for the first time an actual dollar figure for Azure, around $33 billion.

Shares rose about 3%. Microsoft is spending enormously too, with next-quarter capex guided above $50 billion, but it's showing the revenue line that the spend is supposed to produce. Alphabet's Cloud number is doing that job, and it still wasn't enough.

The honest read is that Alphabet is now a hardware company in a way it never was before. TPU systems are a meaningful revenue contributor, which means inventory, working capital swings and lumpy cash flow are part of the model.

That's fine if you're Nvidia and the market prices you that way. Alphabet is still priced like a software business with an ad machine attached, and this quarter is the first time the gap showed up in a number that can't be explained away.

item.title: Talos: KeyDrift Malware Hides in Cisco SD-WAN Controllers to Steal IPsec Keys
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco Talos says an APT it tracks as UAT-11473, with infrastructure overlapping Volt Typhoon, used CVE-2026-20127 to plant implants that hook vdaemon and siphon AES-256 data-plane key material off vSmart controllers.
item.content:encoded:
The implant doesn't steal your traffic. It steals the keys that protect your traffic, which is worse. Cisco Talos published a teardown on October 28 of a malware framework it calls KeyDrift, found on Catalyst SD-WAN controllers compromised through CVE-2026-20127, the CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass Cisco disclosed in February.

Talos attributes the activity to a group it tracks as UAT-11473 and assesses with high confidence that the group's infrastructure overlaps with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network.

KeyDrift has two main pieces. PolyFlame gets injected into the vdaemon process by way of rsshd using ptrace, and a variant hides as the aaamgr service. It interposes socket and DTLS functions so it can take tasking in-band, and it can act as a relay, forwarding command-and-control traffic to other compromised peers.

LittleFilch hooks SSL_read inside vdaemon on vSmart controllers and pulls a 32-byte field that Talos assesses to be the OMP-distributed AES-256 IPsec data-plane key, along with the peer's public IP and system IP.

Think about what that means in an SD-WAN. vSmart distributes the keys every edge router uses to encrypt tunnels. An attacker sitting on that controller, reading those keys as they go by, can decrypt data-plane traffic anywhere in the fabric without ever touching an edge device.

Records get RSA-encrypted, staged in /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and shipped out over UDP dressed up as DTLS 1.2 application-data records. On a controller that's supposed to be talking DTLS all day, that blends in.

The victim list is the tell. Talos names space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research. That's not a ransomware crew's shopping list. It's the profile of a group collecting for a government, and the Volt Typhoon overlap, which Talos is careful to describe as infrastructure rather than a firm identity, points the same direction.

CVE-2026-20127 itself is old news if you patched in February, and Talos previously said the bug had been exploited since at least 2023. The new information is what the attackers did after getting in. If your controllers were exposed before the patch, patching alone doesn't evict an implant that's already injected into vdaemon, and it doesn't rotate keys that were already read.

Talos published Snort rules: SIDs 65938 and 65958 for the CVE, and 67387 through 67416 (Snort 2) or 7:44 through 7:73 (Snort 3) for the malware itself. File paths to hunt for include /tmp/system-vdaemon, /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf and /etc/sv/aaamgr/. No hardcoded IPs or domains were recovered, so there's no easy blocklist. If you find any of it, assume the IPsec keys are burned and rekey the fabric.

item.title: Cisco Patches Second ASA and FTD SSL VPN Zero-Day Since August
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-76418 lets an unauthenticated attacker reload any ASA or FTD firewall running remote-access SSL VPN with secondary authentication, Cisco says it's being exploited, and there's no workaround.
item.content:encoded:
Cisco shipped fixes Wednesday evening for a firewall bug attackers were already using. CVE-2026-76418 is a logic error in the Remote Access SSL VPN service on Secure Firewall ASA and FTD. An unauthenticated remote attacker can force the device to reload.

No VPN login needed, no user interaction, just a reachable webvpn interface and the right configuration on the other side. Cisco scored it 8.6 and says PSIRT became aware of active exploitation sometime in October.

The configuration that matters is secondary authentication on a tunnel group. If webvpn is enabled on at least one interface and any tunnel group, including DefaultWEBVPNGroup, has secondary authentication configured, you're exposed. The tunnel-group-list setting changes which groups an attacker can reach but doesn't make you safe. Cloud-delivered Firewall, cloud FMC, Secure Access and Secure FMC aren't affected.

This is the second time since August that someone has found a way to crash these boxes through the VPN service. CVE-2026-20349, also 8.6, was an HTTP request handling flaw in the same service and was also exploited before Cisco knew about it. Cisco never said who was behind that one. It hasn't said who's behind this one either.

Two unattributed DoS zero-days in the same service inside three months is a pattern, not a coincidence. Somebody is spending real effort on knocking Cisco edge firewalls offline, and a reload on a remote-access VPN concentrator is not a minor nuisance. For a lot of organizations that's every remote worker dropping at once, and if the attacker can do it on a loop, it's an outage.

Fixed ASA releases are 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1. Fixed FTD releases are 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1. Cisco lists no workaround. The only mitigations are to remove secondary authentication from affected tunnel groups or disable the tunnel group list, and Cisco notes both lower your security posture. That's a bad trade for most shops, so plan the upgrade instead.

One practical note. If you patched for CVE-2026-20349 in August and assumed the VPN service was clean, that patch doesn't cover this. Check your running version against the list above, and if you've seen unexplained reloads on an ASA or FTD this month, that's your indicator.

item.title: CISA Puts a CVSS 2.7 ESXi Logging Bug on KEV After China-Linked Zero-Day Use
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-41709 lets an ESXi admin run operations that never hit the logs, CrowdStrike says WARP PANDA used it as a zero-day inside U.S. law firms, and federal agencies have until November 11 to patch.
item.content:encoded:
A CVSS 2.7 bug just landed on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and that score is the whole point of the story. CVE-2026-41709 is an insufficient-logging flaw in VMware ESX. An attacker who already holds administrator access can perform certain operations on the hypervisor without those operations being recorded.

Broadcom rated it Low, fixed it in VMSA-2026-0006 back on July 29, and credited Ian Barton of CrowdStrike for the find. Nobody would have put it at the top of a patch queue.

CrowdStrike's 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report explains why it belongs there. The firm says WARP PANDA, a China-nexus espionage group that nearly always goes after U.S.-based law firms, exploited the flaw as a zero-day in several intrusions, as late as early 2026. The group had already planted malware in victims' vCenter environments. The logging bypass wasn't the way in. It was the way to stay quiet once inside.

That's an unusual profile for a KEV entry. Most catalog additions are remote code execution or auth bypass, the bugs that get an attacker in. This one is pure anti-forensics. If your incident response plan assumes ESXi audit logs are a reliable record of what an admin did, this bug breaks that assumption for anyone who got admin credentials by other means. Which, for a group that lives in vCenter, is the normal case.

Neither Broadcom nor CrowdStrike has said which operations go unlogged. The advisory doesn't list them, and the KEV entry doesn't describe the observed exploitation. Broadcom's advisory page still doesn't mention in-the-wild use at all. That's a gap defenders deserve to have filled, because without it you can't know which log sources to cross-check against.

The fix is straightforward. Broadcom's fixed builds are ESXi80U3j-25429389 for 8.0, ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025 for 9.0, and ESXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 for 9.1. VMware Cloud Foundation and Telco Cloud Platform have separate guidance, and anyone still on 7.0 extended support has to go through Broadcom support. There is no workaround. CISA's deadline for federal agencies is November 11, 2026, and the KEV entry lists ransomware use as unknown.

If you run ESXi and skipped the July advisory because the headline CVEs didn't apply to you, go back and look. VMSA-2026-0006 also carried two 9.8 vCenter bugs and a 9.3 VMXNET3 escape, so a host that's missing this patch is probably missing those too. And if you've had any vCenter or ESXi compromise this year, treat the hypervisor logs from that window as incomplete rather than clean.

item.title: Genie 4 Adds Native Audio and Live Scene Edits, for Trusted Testers Only
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google DeepMind's new world model generates sound alongside its interactive video and lets users rewrite a scene mid-simulation by typing, but the launch post gives no resolution, frame rate, or consistency figures and almost nobody can use it yet.
item.content:encoded:
Google DeepMind's Genie 4 generates a playable world from a prompt, lets you walk around in it, and now scores it with sound as you go: ambient noise, music, and dialogue from the characters you meet. That's the headline from the October 27 announcement, and it's a real step. Previous Genie models were silent films.

The other new trick is live steering. You can type an instruction mid-simulation, like moving the camera, changing the weather, or dropping in a new character, and the world adjusts without restarting. DeepMind says a model it calls Gemini Omni keeps the simulation anchored to how things actually look and behave in the real world, with other Gemini models supplying the reasoning that holds a scene together over time.

Here is what the post doesn't say. There's no resolution, no frame rate, no number for how long a world stays consistent, no parameter count, and no stated limitations.

Genie 3's announcement last year quoted 720p at 24 frames per second and talked about consistency over a few minutes. Several secondary outlets are repeating a two-minute consistency figure for Genie 4, but it isn't in Google's text, so treat it as rumor until Google writes it down.

Access is narrow. Genie 4 is rolling out now to a limited group of trusted testers. Google AI Ultra subscribers get it "soon" inside Project Genie, and early access partners will see it through the Gemini API and AI Studio. No price, no date for general availability.

DeepMind frames all of this as a path to AGI, with simulation as a training ground for robots and software agents, plus creative uses in film, games, journalism, and manufacturing. The robotics argument is the strongest one.

If a model can produce physically plausible, interactive environments on demand, you can train an agent on a million kitchens without building one. The creative-tools pitch is weaker, because a demo reel and a production pipeline are very different things, and nothing in this release is a production pipeline.

Call it what it is: an impressive research preview with a marketing post attached. The audio is new, the steering is new, and the specs are missing. When the Gemini API access actually opens and developers can measure it, we'll know whether the realism claims hold up outside of DeepMind's own clips.

item.title: Amazon's New Echos: a $250 Speaker With a Camera and a $200 Sleep-Sensing Clock
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Amazon's fall hardware refresh adds a camera to the Echo Studio, a camera-free Echo Time alarm clock that watches your sleep instead, a 10-inch Alexa Photo Frame, and a $500 Echo Show 16.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon's answer to the question of what Alexa+ needs next is more sensors in more rooms. The five devices it introduced on October 28 put a camera on the kitchen speaker, sleep sensing on the nightstand, and a 16-inch screen on the wall.

The headline oddity is the Echo Studio with Home Camera at $249.99, shipping today. It's the Dolby Atmos speaker with a camera bolted on, pitched for room check-ins from the Alexa app and for showing Alexa a physical object, like a board game, and having it explain the rules.

Amazon says video calling through compatible Fire TVs is coming. The camera-free Echo Studio sticks around at $219.99. Engadget reports the camera is live-view only and doesn't record footage, which is the privacy line Amazon will lean on when people ask why their speaker has eyes.

Echo Time is the more interesting product. It's a $199.99 bedside clock with a small round display and, deliberately, no camera. The pitch is sleep sensing through what Amazon brands Omnisense: it detects when you're in lighter sleep and wakes you within a 10-to-60-minute window before your alarm, no wearable needed.

Bloomberg reported that sleep sensing is off by default, and the clock carries a National Sleep Foundation SleepMark. Hundreds of clock faces and a sunrise-style gradual brightening round it out. A Kids version runs $209.99 with a year of Kids+.

The rest of the lineup: a new Echo Dot at $99.99 with Amazon's AZ3 chip, four microphones, a built-in Zigbee, Thread, and Matter hub, and an eero Wi-Fi extender that covers about 1,000 square feet. An Alexa Photo Frame with a 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen at $200 in black or $229 in birch or walnut, synced to Amazon Photos.

And the Echo Show 16, a wall-hung 16-inch display with built-in Fire TV, a 13-megapixel night-vision camera, and a new Alexa Home Map view, from $499.99 or $569.99 with the Nanomatte panel. It's preorder only with $100 off and ships by year end.

Every device runs the new Alexa, and Amazon is clear that certain features need Alexa+, which comes with Prime. That's the actual strategy here. Amazon says hundreds of millions of customers now use the new Alexa experiences and talk to it two to three times more than before. The hardware exists to give that assistant more context, and more context means more microphones, a camera, and a sensor that knows when you're asleep.

Whether a $250 speaker with a camera finds a market is a fair question. Amazon tried a version of this with the Echo Look years ago and quietly killed it. The difference this time is that the assistant on the other end can actually do something with what it sees.

item.title: Meta Prices a $25B Share Sale at $625 to Fund a $97.5B AI Capital Plan
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta upsized its Class A offering to $25 billion and added $12.5 billion of 6.5% mandatory convertible preferred, the first two legs of a roughly $97.5 billion equity program to pay for data centers.
item.content:encoded:
Meta sold $25 billion of its own stock on Tuesday at $625 a share, and the shares closed the day at $620.19. Buyers paid a premium to own a piece of the most expensive capital spending plan in the company's history.

The deal got bigger as it went. Meta started at $22.5 billion of Class A common and raised it to $25 billion after demand came in at roughly five times the shares on offer, according to people familiar with the sale who spoke to Bloomberg.

Alongside it, Meta priced 250 million depositary shares at $50 each in a 6.50% Series A mandatory convertible preferred, good for about $12.5 billion net, with a 30-day option for underwriters to take another 37.5 million. Both pieces are set to close October 29.

There's a wrinkle in the common stock leg that most of the headlines skipped. It's structured as forward sale agreements with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. Meta doesn't bank the roughly $24.9 billion until those agreements settle, which the prospectus says will happen on or before November 19, 2027.

The banks borrow and sell the shares now; Meta delivers its own shares and collects later. It locks in today's price without flooding the market with new shares immediately.

The third leg is still to come: about $60 billion through an at-the-market program in Class C non-voting shares, scheduled for early 2027. Add it up and you get the $97.5 billion figure. Nvidia and AMD have separately said they'll put a combined $4 billion into the company.

All of this is to pay for compute. Meta has guided 2026 capital expenditures to between $135 billion and $145 billion, roughly double the $72.2 billion it spent in 2025. For years the company funded expansion out of a cash machine; now it's selling equity in tens-of-billions blocks, which is what you do when the cash machine can't keep up with the ambition.

The dilution math is what shareholders will chew on. The common stock alone is about 40 million new shares, and the preferred converts into more later. Issuing non-voting Class C for the biggest tranche keeps Mark Zuckerberg's control intact while spreading the economic cost across everyone else, which is a very Meta way to raise $97 billion.

item.title: An Israeli Ad Firm Outbid Everyone for Starlink Users' Ads in 105 Countries
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Reuters reports that the actor Trend Micro's TrendAI unit called SHADOW-EARTH-79 is Discover-Tech, a company that used programmatic ad auctions to win a disproportionate share of Starlink traffic, including in countries where the service is banned.
item.content:encoded:
Every time a web page loads an ad, an auction runs in the background, and the bidders get to see things about the device on the other end: its IP address, network identifiers, an advertising ID, and sometimes location. Win enough of those auctions for a specific population and you've built a tracking system without touching a single piece of malware. According to a Reuters report on October 27, that's what an Israeli firm did to Starlink users.

The underlying research came from TrendAI, the rebranded research arm of Trend Micro, on October 15. Its report described an actor it labeled SHADOW-EARTH-79 that was the leading winning bidder for observed Starlink ad traffic in 105 countries.

The numbers are stark on their face: the actor took 12.9% of Starlink ad impressions in the dataset against 2.6% of overall traffic. The report named no company. Reuters, citing six people familiar with the research, says the codename refers to Discover-Tech, and five of those sources said legal concerns were the reason executives left the name out.

Why would anyone want Starlink users specifically? Think about who relies on a satellite terminal rather than a local ISP. Starlink is restricted or banned in a long list of countries, and the people using it there tend to be interesting to intelligence services: activists, journalists, military units, and smugglers alike.

A terminal's IP block tells you the user is on Starlink. The rest of the ad auction data helps narrow down where and who.

The report has limits, and Trend Micro says so. The data comes from a single ad-buying platform, and IP-based country estimates carry real uncertainty. Nothing here shows Starlink's network or satellites were breached. Receiving an ad from a suspect bidder also doesn't mean a device was compromised. What it shows is intent and scale, which in this corner of the industry is usually enough to act on.

Discover-Tech isn't new to this conversation. Citizen Lab and the ad-fraud firm Confiant both named the company publicly on October 15 in connection with the same ad-based targeting, and Google, Comcast, and other platform operators have reportedly removed it from their ad exchanges. SpaceX, Discover-Tech, and its chief executive didn't respond to Reuters.

The real-time bidding system was designed to sell shoes faster. It leaks enough to geolocate a satellite dish in a war zone. That's a design problem for the ad industry, not a Starlink problem, and no one in the ad industry is in a hurry to fix it.

item.title: Attackers Are Already Probing Oracle EBS's New CVSS 9.8 SQL Injection Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Defused Cyber's decoys logged exploit attempts against CVE-2026-101767 on Monday morning, one week after Oracle's October patch batch and a year after Cl0p's last E-Business Suite campaign.
item.content:encoded:
One week. That's how long it took for someone to start throwing exploit traffic at Oracle E-Business Suite installs after Oracle shipped the fix for CVE-2026-101767 in its October 20 Critical Patch Update. Defused Cyber said its EBS decoys recorded what it called exploratory exploits on the morning of October 27.

The bug is an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet, reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer inside the Application Object Library component. Horizon3.ai researchers Brandon Peterson, Jimi Sebree, and Noah King found it and reported it to Oracle on July 24.

Their write-up explains the chain: a crafted request runs SQL as the APPS database user, and from there you can get operating system command execution as the EBS application account. Oracle scores it CVSS 9.8. Affected versions run from 12.2.3 through 12.2.15.

Nobody has shown a production compromise yet. What Defused saw were probes against honeypots, and Oracle hasn't marked the CVE as exploited in the wild. CISA hadn't added it to the KEV catalog as of Tuesday. Treat that as a gap in confirmation, not a reason to relax.

The reason to take this seriously is the recent history. A year ago, Cl0p ran a mass extortion campaign against EBS customers using CVE-2025-61882, another unauthenticated path to code execution, and worked through the victim list for weeks.

EBS sits in finance and HR back offices at large organizations, often behind a thin web tier that someone exposed to the internet years ago for supplier portals. It's exactly the kind of target where a one-week lag between patch and probe matters, because the patch cycle for EBS at most shops is measured in quarters.

Don't confuse this with the other critical EBS fix in the same CPU. Oracle's October release addressed nearly 1,300 issues across its product line, and one of the EBS Workflow flaws carries a CVSS 10.0. Different bug, different component. Both need the patch.

Horizon3 published indicators worth loading into your detection stack today: unauthenticated POST requests to AppsTCFServer that instantiate the GanttDataServer class, followed by database activity; reconnaissance queries for the database version, current user, and directory objects; unexpected files appearing in $APPLPTMP; and the oracle account spawning /bin/sh via Concurrent Manager. If you can't patch this week, pull /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer out of the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict the web tier to networks you trust.

item.title: Magento's PolyShell Lands on CISA KEV, Seven Months After Attacks Began
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-48356 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on Tuesday with a November 10 deadline, long after Sansec watched attackers plant PHP backdoors on most of the Magento stores it monitors.
item.content:encoded:
Sansec warned the Magento world about PolyShell on March 17. Attackers started using it two days later. By mid-April, more than 80% of the stores Sansec protects had seen malicious PHP uploads aimed at the bug. On October 27, CISA finally put it on the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The flaw is CVE-2026-48356, an unrestricted file upload in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source that Adobe scores at CVSS 9.3. An unauthenticated attacker calls the REST guest-cart route, the one at /V1/guest-carts/{cartId}/items, and attaches a file as a custom product option. Magento writes it to pub/media/custom_options/quote/ after checking only that it starts with a valid image header.

So the attackers send a polyglot: a file with a real GIF or PNG header and PHP code behind it, typically named something like index.php. On a stock nginx install from the 2.0 through 2.2 era, or any non-stock config that hands .php files under media to FastCGI, that upload executes.

Adobe fixed it in Magento 2.4.9 on May 12 and backported the fix to the 2.4.4 through 2.4.8 lines in security bulletin APSB26-73 on July 14. Those are the "2026-jul" builds. Anything older than those on any branch is still exposed.

What's happening on compromised stores isn't subtle. Sansec describes a backdoor called accesson.php copied into assets/images/ folders across multiple directories, with beaconing, eval-based command execution, and further upload capability. On top of that, an obfuscated JavaScript loader gets injected into CMS pages or static blocks, persists itself in the browser's localStorage, and pulls follow-on payloads from lanhd6549tdhse[.]top.

Sansec tied one PolyShell intrusion in March to a WebRTC-based card skimmer on a retailer it describes as worth more than $100 billion. Several write-ups this week note Adobe's bulletin still doesn't flag the bug as exploited, which says something about how disconnected vendor advisories can be from what's actually happening on the ground.

The KEV timing is the uncomfortable part. Seven months passed between mass exploitation and a federal mandate, and the November 10 deadline under BOD 26-04 now lands on agencies for a bug whose public proof of concept has been sitting on GitHub for months. KEV is supposed to be the signal that tells overworked teams what to patch first. It worked as a lagging indicator here.

CISA added a second entry the same day: CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder bug behind the Node2Shell and Broccoli2Shell headlines, also due November 10. Honeypot operators Previdian and ELLIO have each logged exploit attempts against it, and one of the source IPs was also throwing PHP2Shell traffic. Node.js shipped fixes in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 with no workaround.

If you run Magento or Adobe Commerce, patching is step one, not the whole job. Search pub/media/custom_options/ for anything ending in .php, .phtml, or .phar. Hunt for accesson.php across the document root. Grep CMS content for the loader domains Sansec published. Then block script execution under pub/media/ at the web server, because the next upload bug in this codebase is a matter of when.

item.title: Microsoft Offers Buyouts to 60,000 People Two Days Before Earnings
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Roughly a quarter of Microsoft's workforce can take a tenure-based severance and leave December 31, as the company's AI capex climbs toward $145 billion for the fiscal year.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty thousand Microsoft employees, a bit over a quarter of the company, got an offer on Monday: leave on December 31 with a tenure-based severance package, or stay. Decisions are due the first week of December. Microsoft reports fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday, and nobody should pretend the timing is a coincidence.

The offer covers employees up to vice president level in the US, UK, Canada and India, with other countries handled under local law. In the US the floor is eight weeks of pay, plus continued stock vesting, health coverage and career services; a spokesperson told Fortune the terms match Microsoft's standard separation packages.

It's the second such program this year. The first, in April, was limited to long-tenured staff and was the first voluntary buyout Microsoft had ever offered.

Chief people officer Amy Coleman's memo frames it as giving people 'a new choice to make that transition now with support.' That's the kindest available reading of a program whose other name is headcount reduction without a layoff headline.

The money explains the rest. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capital expenditures in the June quarter and has projected about $145 billion in total spending for fiscal 2026, almost all of it data centers for AI capacity that Azure keeps selling out of.

Headcount was about 223,000 at the end of June, down 5,000 from a year earlier, and the company cut roughly 4,800 jobs in July, most of them in Xbox. Every dollar of salary that walks out the door voluntarily is a dollar that never shows up as a restructuring charge.

How many will take it? Asked that, the spokesperson pointed to peer programs with 3% to 5% uptake. On 60,000 people that's 1,800 to 3,000, a rounding error against the capex line and a smaller cut than July's. If that's really the expectation, the program is as much a message for Wednesday's call as it is an org-chart change.

If uptake comes in higher, the people most likely to leave are the ones with the most tenure and the best outside options, which is the opposite of what an efficiency push wants.

The 60,000 figure comes from a person familiar with the program, not from Microsoft, and the company hasn't published a target. Listen on Wednesday for whether anyone on Microsoft's side says the number out loud.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra Is a Computer-Use Model at $1 In, $5 Out
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The new mid-tier model halves GPT-5.6 Terra's price, posts OpenAI-reported gains on Terminal-Bench and OSWorld, and carries a 'Critical' cybersecurity rating under the Preparedness Framework.
item.content:encoded:
A dollar per million input tokens, five per million out. That's the price of GPT-6.1 Terra, the model OpenAI shipped Monday to replace GPT-5.6 Terra as its mid-tier, and it's half what the outgoing model charged for input and well under half for output.

It's also half the list price of GPT-6.1 Sol. The pitch isn't that Terra is the smartest model in the lineup. It's that it's the cheapest one you'd trust to click around a desktop unattended.

Terra's job is the boring middle of knowledge work: read a screen, fill a form, process an invoice, switch between apps, draft the proposal, pull a shot log out of a video. OpenAI slots it below Sol and Astra and above Luna, and says plainly that you should still reach for Sol or Astra for the hardest coding tasks. Cached input is listed at five cents per million, and third-party model docs put the context window just over a million tokens.

The benchmark claims are OpenAI's own and nobody has reproduced them yet. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 at max effort, Terra scores 50.3% against GPT-5.6 Terra's published 21.5%. On OSWorld 2.1, the computer-use benchmark, OpenAI says the medium-effort score beats the old model's best setting.

On its internal error-inducing prompt test, the low-effort error rate drops from 53.6% to 16.7%, and to 4.3% at max. What those tests measure is task completion in sandboxed environments with known answers. What they don't measure is what happens when the invoice is wrong.

The comparison OpenAI most wanted you to see is the one against Claude Opus 5.5: on its Agents' Last Exam benchmark at max effort, about a ninth of the cost per task, from a mix of a lower token price and fewer tokens burned. That's a pricing argument more than a capability one, and it's aimed squarely at the agent builders who've been quietly standardizing on Anthropic.

Terra carries a 'Critical' rating for cybersecurity capability under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, the same level as GPT-6 Astra, and ships with the same mitigations. This is the first release in the family since OpenAI cancelled GPT-6.1 Astra last month after it failed internal safety testing. A cheaper computer-use model clearing the bar while a bigger one didn't tells you where the line gets drawn: on what the model can do with a terminal, not on how large it is.

It's live for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu, in Codex, and through the API as gpt-6.1-terra. If you've got an agent running on GPT-5.6 Terra, the swap is a config change and the bill drops by half. Run your own eval first. The headline per-token price is for text, and a model that reads screenshots all day burns input tokens in ways the pricing page doesn't put on the front.

item.title: Apple Backports the CoreGraphics Zero-Day Fix to iPhone XS and XR, a Month Late
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
